name: The Ledger Tyrant
description: Rules by accounting rather than cruelty, punishing every debt and slight with exact proportion, and genuinely believes that a perfectly balanced book is the same thing as justice.
hook: Rules by accounting rather than cruelty, punishing every debt and slight with exact proportion, and genuinely believes that a perfectly balanced book is the same thing as justice.
seen_by_others: Feared more than hated; people say this lord never shouts, never forgets, and will hang a man for a missing sack as calmly as signing a charter.
habits: Carries a wax tablet listing who owes what, recites sums aloud during audiences, and inspects the tax tallies personally at the end of every season.
secrets: Once miscounted a fine, hanged an innocent man for it, and never corrected the record.
Cannot sleep unless the household accounts balance to the last copper coin.
Keeps a dead mother's unpaid debts on a separate page and pays them in secret.
lines: State your name, your business, and what you can offer. In that order, please.
Three sheep short, two seasons running. The village will pay four, and learn arithmetic.
Wars are only debts collected with steel. I prefer my collectors cheaper.
Noted. Every insult has a price, and I always collect what I am owed.
Praise costs you nothing, so it is worth exactly that to me.
Forty and twelve, less the tithe... no. Again. It must balance.

name: The Reluctant Heir
description: Raised for the cloister and the library, then thrust into lordship when an older brother died, and still answers every crisis by wishing someone else were in charge.
hook: Raised for the cloister and the library, then thrust into lordship when an older brother died, and still answers every crisis by wishing someone else were in charge.
seen_by_others: Servants find this heir kind but useless; vassals whisper that the wrong child lived, and some already make plans around them.
habits: Hides in the chapel or the library when petitioners arrive, signs orders without reading them, and asks advisers what the dead brother would have done.
secrets: Felt relieved, for one shameful moment, on hearing that the brother had died.
Has written a letter abdicating the claim and keeps it unsent inside a book.
Practises with the sword at night, badly, so that nobody can see and laugh.
lines: Oh. Good day. Are you here to see me? Surely there is someone more suitable.
The steward says I must judge this dispute. Must I? Very well, tell me slowly.
My brother would have ridden out already. I am still deciding which boot goes first.
Yes, I know. I have heard it said better, by people who matter more.
You are very kind. Wrong, but kind. Please do not repeat it before my vassals.
One more year. Then I will find a cousin who actually wants this.

name: The Wine-Soaked Lord
description: Once the sharpest commander of a generation, now drowning the memory of one catastrophic defeat in wine every night, and brilliant for exactly one hour each morning.
hook: Once the sharpest commander of a generation, now drowning the memory of one catastrophic defeat in wine every night, and brilliant for exactly one hour each morning.
seen_by_others: Old soldiers defend this lord fiercely; younger nobles mock the stumbling and the smell, and nobody dares call a council after noon.
habits: Keeps a cup within reach from midday on, tells the same battle story with shifting details, and walks the walls before dawn, grey and silent.
secrets: Gave the order that lost that battle, though another man took the blame.
Has tried to stop drinking four times and hidden every failure from the family.
Still writes every winter to the widow of an old standard-bearer.
lines: Sit, sit. Pour yourself one. No, pour me one, you look like you need to watch.
Ask me before noon and you get a general. After noon you get a story. Choose.
Kings love a war until the first burial. Then they love blaming the man who fought it.
Say it again when I am sober, boy, and see whether you keep your teeth.
I was good, once. Now I am merely loud. Thank you all the same.
Left flank. Always the left flank. Why did I not see the left flank.

name: The Almsgiving Saint
description: Gives away grain, coin and even her own cloak to every beggar who asks, starving her household coffers, and is quietly proud of being so much humbler than everyone else.
hook: Gives away grain, coin and even her own cloak to every beggar who asks, starving her household coffers, and is quietly proud of being so much humbler than everyone else.
seen_by_others: The poor call her blessed and kiss her hem; her steward calls her a slow disaster, and her children have learned to hide their good clothes.
habits: Waits at the gate every morning with bread, fasts loudly on holy days, and gently corrects anyone who spends money on themselves in her presence.
secrets: Keeps one jewelled ring hidden that she has never managed to give away.
Enjoys being thanked far more than she enjoys the giving itself.
Once refused alms to a woman she simply disliked, and still dreams of it.
lines: Welcome, friend. Have you eaten? Do not lie to me, I can see that you have not.
The granary is for the hungry, not for the steward's ledgers. Open it.
Lords wage war for land. The land belongs to the hungry who work it.
I forgive you. I will pray for you, too, at some length, in public.
Oh, I am no saint. Though the priest did say something very similar on holy day.
Give it away. Give it away. Why does it feel so sweet to say no?

name: The Gilded Coward
description: Tells magnificent tales of personal courage at every feast, wears battle-scarred armour bought secondhand, and has never once been anywhere near the front of a charge.
hook: Tells magnificent tales of personal courage at every feast, wears battle-scarred armour bought secondhand, and has never once been anywhere near the front of a charge.
seen_by_others: Peers roll their eyes at the stories; the soldiers know exactly where this lord stands in battle, and rather like being kept out of danger.
habits: Polishes an unused sword before company, arrives at battles late with excellent excuses, and asks scouts three times whether the enemy is really gone.
secrets: The famous scar on the cheek came from falling off a pony at twelve.
Paid a minstrel to compose a song about a skirmish spent hiding in a ditch.
Keeps a fast horse saddled at all times, day and night, just in case.
lines: Ah, a traveller! You may have heard of me. The bridge at, well, a bridge. Famous.
My men are held in reserve. Reserve is a vital position. The most vital, really.
War? I adore war. From a sensible distance, with a good map and a tent.
How dare you. I would challenge you, but my physician has forbidden exertion.
Brave? Yes. Yes, I suppose I am. Tell the others, would you.
They will not come tonight. They cannot. Check the horse again.

name: The Impatient Reformer
description: Determined to drag the realm out of old custom with roads, abolished tolls and an end to serf dues, crushing anyone too slow to be grateful for the improvements.
hook: Determined to drag the realm out of old custom with roads, abolished tolls and an end to serf dues, crushing anyone too slow to be grateful for the improvements.
seen_by_others: Merchants praise the new roads; peasants fear the surveyors, and the old families predict that vassals will strangle this lord within five years.
habits: Rewrites village charters by hand, interrupts petitioners to explain a better system, and tours the estates unannounced to catch officials in old ways.
secrets: The first reform caused a famine in two villages, and the headmen took the blame.
Fears privately that the reforms are only vanity dressed up as virtue.
Copied most of the ideas from a book they claim never to have read.
lines: Good, a fresh face. Tell me what is broken where you come from, and I will fix it.
The toll is abolished. Yes, today. No, I do not care who collected it before.
Old lords guard old ways because the old ways feed them. I intend to starve them.
Call me what you like. In ten years your children will cross my bridge.
Do not praise me. Help me. Praise builds nothing at all.
Why does everything take so long. Why does everyone want permission.

name: The Smiling Schemer
description: Never refuses anyone to their face, agrees warmly with every faction at once, and quietly plays each against the others until every possible outcome somehow ends up serving them.
hook: Never refuses anyone to their face, agrees warmly with every faction at once, and quietly plays each against the others until every possible outcome somehow ends up serving them.
seen_by_others: Everyone considers them a dear friend, which is precisely the problem; the shrewd ones count their fingers after every handshake.
habits: Remembers the names of everyone's children, sends small gifts after every quarrel, and writes letters late at night that nobody ever sees sent.
secrets: Keeps a coded list of every favour owed and every lie told.
Has genuinely forgotten what they themselves actually want from life.
Wept once, alone, when a friend they had betrayed simply forgave them.
lines: What a pleasure. Truly. Sit, tell me everything, I am terribly curious about you.
Of course I support the proposal. I support the other one too. Both have merit.
The powerful are just people who have not yet noticed who arranged their power.
Oh, how wonderful, you are honest. I shall remember that about you. Fondly.
You flatter me. Now tell me what you want, and we will both enjoy this more.
Three letters tonight. No, four. The fourth one must arrive late.

name: The Weary Crown
description: Has ruled so long and buried so many that every decision feels like the hundredth repetition, longing openly for peace while signing yet another call to arms.
hook: Has ruled so long and buried so many that every decision feels like the hundredth repetition, longing openly for peace while signing yet another call to arms.
seen_by_others: Courtiers say the crown has grown heavy; enemies smell weakness, and loyal vassals worry about who will decide anything once the sighing stops.
habits: Takes long pauses before answering, rubs their temples through every council, and walks alone among the graves of their own children at dusk.
secrets: Has drafted terms of surrender twice and burned them both times.
Can no longer picture the face of a first spouse without real effort.
Envies the gravediggers, who at least get to finish their work each day.
lines: Another traveller. Welcome. Whatever you have come to tell me, I have probably heard it.
Yes, raise the levies. Again. Tell the villages I am sorry. Again.
Every king I outlived was certain this war would be the last. Every one.
You may be right. I am too tired to have you flogged for it.
Kind words. I used to collect them. Now I just let them pass.
One more winter. Then perhaps they will let me sit in the sun.

name: The Mirror Lord
description: Measures every day by how he looked during it, spends a village's taxes on silks and portraits, and takes a lost battle less personally than a ruined cloak.
hook: Measures every day by how he looked during it, spends a village's taxes on silks and portraits, and takes a lost battle less personally than a ruined cloak.
seen_by_others: Tailors adore him and soldiers despise him; ladies at court laugh behind their fans, yet copy whatever he wore last season.
habits: Checks his reflection in polished shields and goblets, changes clothes three times a day, and positions himself in the best light at every audience.
secrets: He is going bald and wears an artful cap to hide it.
He was a plain, mocked child and still hears the old nicknames at night.
He once had a painter whipped for painting him exactly as he looked.
lines: Stand there. No, there, out of my light. Now you may speak.
The tax will fund the new hall. A lord must be seen to be a lord.
The king wore green at the last feast. Green. Can you imagine it.
Say what you like of me, but you will remember my face. Will anyone remember yours?
Go on. Go on. You have an eye, I can tell. Continue.
The left side is better. It has always been the left side.

name: The Storybook Knight
description: A young noble raised on tales of perfect knights, who keeps vows nobody asked for, challenges grown men over imagined slights, and cannot understand why the world refuses to behave like a song.
hook: A young noble raised on tales of perfect knights, who keeps vows nobody asked for, challenges grown men over imagined slights, and cannot understand why the world refuses to behave like a song.
seen_by_others: Elders find him charming and exhausting; seasoned soldiers place bets on how long his ideals will survive his first real battle.
habits: Recites oaths before meals, rescues people who did not need rescuing, and keeps a little book of the noble deeds he still intends to perform.
secrets: He froze completely during his first skirmish and has told no one.
He has never actually read the tales he quotes, only heard them sung.
He is secretly in love with someone far below his station.
lines: Good stranger, if any wrong has been done you, name it, and I shall right it.
A knight protects the weak. That is the whole of it. Why does everyone make it complicated?
If the king commands an unjust thing, a true knight must refuse. Must he not?
You will retract that, sir, or meet me in the yard at dawn.
Truly? You think me a true knight? I shall try to deserve it.
They never sing about the smell. Why do they never sing about the smell?

name: The Bitter Second Son
description: Born an hour too late to inherit anything, more capable than the brother who did, and every loyal service he renders is laced with a resentment he cannot swallow.
hook: Born an hour too late to inherit anything, more capable than the brother who did, and every loyal service he renders is laced with a resentment he cannot swallow.
seen_by_others: People say he would make the better lord, which only makes it worse; his brother trusts him completely and really should not.
habits: Quietly corrects his brother's orders afterwards, counts the heir's mistakes aloud over wine, and refuses every lesser title he is offered.
secrets: He once hesitated a long moment before warning his brother of an ambush.
He loves his brother's children more than his brother does.
He keeps a map of the family lands with his own name written over them.
lines: You will want my brother. Everyone wants my brother. I am merely the one who knows things.
The orders come from him. The work comes from me. That is how this house runs.
Inheritance is the cruellest lottery. The prize goes to whoever was quickest to be born.
Careful. I am not the heir, so I have nothing to lose by answering that.
Better than him? Say it louder. No, do not. Say it never.
One hour. One hour, and everything would have been mine.

name: The Iron Matriarch
description: Holds a scattered clan together through sheer will, choosing every marriage, alliance and punishment herself, and has never once let anyone she loves see her tired.
hook: Holds a scattered clan together through sheer will, choosing every marriage, alliance and punishment herself, and has never once let anyone she loves see her tired.
seen_by_others: Her sons obey her even as grown lords; her daughters-in-law dread her, and rival clans negotiate with her, never with the men.
habits: Sits at the head of the table whoever is lord, keeps the household keys on her belt, and visits the nursery every night to inspect the heirs.
secrets: She poisoned a rival's prize horse decades ago and never confessed it.
She was terrified on her wedding day and still despises the girl she was.
She cries for her dead firstborn only in the cellar, among the wine barrels.
lines: Whose child are you? Never mind. Stand up straight while you answer me.
My son leads the clan. I lead my son. Do not confuse the two.
Kings come and go. Families endure, if someone in them has a spine.
Many have said worse to me, and I have buried most of them.
Flattery is for girls with no dowry. Tell me something useful.
Not yet. Not yet. They are not ready to manage without me.

name: The Open-Handed Ruin
description: Throws feasts, gifts horses to strangers and pays every soldier double, because being loved is the only thing they truly enjoy, even as their treasury quietly bleeds to death.
hook: Throws feasts, gifts horses to strangers and pays every soldier double, because being loved is the only thing they truly enjoy, even as their treasury quietly bleeds to death.
seen_by_others: Everyone adores them and nobody lends them money; their steward has aged ten years in three, and the heirs dread reading the will.
habits: Gives away whatever a guest compliments, orders another feast whenever the hall falls quiet, and waves away every account the steward brings.
secrets: Has secretly mortgaged the ancestral hall to a moneylender in town.
Is terrified that without the gifts nobody would ever visit at all.
Once gave away a horse that their dead father had loved dearly.
lines: A guest! Bring wine, bring the good wine, bring the other good wine too.
Pay the men double. They fought well. Did they? Well, pay them anyway.
A lord who hoards is a lord who is hated. Better to be poor and toasted.
You think me a fool? Have a cup on the fool, then, and think it warmly.
You like the cloak? Take it. No, take it. I insist, I always insist.
Tomorrow I will look at the accounts. Tomorrow, certainly.

name: The Sleepless Lord
description: Survived one poisoning attempt and now sees assassins in every cup, gift and smile, changing bedchambers nightly and trusting no one who has ever been kind to them.
hook: Survived one poisoning attempt and now sees assassins in every cup, gift and smile, changing bedchambers nightly and trusting no one who has ever been kind to them.
seen_by_others: Their court is quiet and frightened; cooks quit, guests leave early, and rivals send gifts purely for the pleasure of watching them refused.
habits: Makes a taster sip from every cup, sleeps in a different room each night, and studies a visitor's hands before letting them come near.
secrets: The poisoning may have been ordinary bad fish, which they will never admit.
Has quietly had a loyal servant killed on nothing more than suspicion.
Sleeps best, oddly, in the stables among the horses and the grooms.
lines: Stop there. Show me your hands. Both of them. Now we may talk.
Who prepared this? Who carried it? Who touched the door? Then nobody eats.
The powerful are not killed in battle. They are killed at dinner.
An insult? Good. An insult is honest. It is kindness I cannot trust.
Why do you praise me? What do you want? Who sent you here?
The latch. Did I check the latch. I checked the latch.

name: The Penitent Warlord
description: Burned whole towns as a young commander, now kneels in chapel every night and endows monasteries, yet still rides to war the moment a cause seems holy enough.
hook: Burned whole towns as a young commander, now kneels in chapel every night and endows monasteries, yet still rides to war the moment a cause seems holy enough.
seen_by_others: Priests praise their generosity, widows of the burned towns curse their name, and soldiers note that penance has never once slowed their sword.
habits: Wears a hair shirt beneath fine clothes, kneels in prayer before and after every battle, and pays for prayers for the dead by the hundred.
secrets: Still remembers the exact number of houses burned, and recites it nightly.
Fears the penance is only a bargain with heaven, not true repentance.
Part of them misses the war, and that part frightens them most.
lines: Peace be with you, stranger. I have none myself, but I can wish it upon you.
The levy rides at dawn. Pray with us first, or ride behind us.
A war fought for heaven fills the same graves. I know. I dug many.
Strike me, if you wish. I have earned worse, and from better people.
Do not call me good. Call me sorry. That is closer to the truth.
Forgive me. Forgive me. And then forgive me tomorrow, too.

name: The Absent Huntsman
description: Happiest in the forest with dogs and a boar spear, he treats government as an irritating interruption between hunts, and knows his hounds' names better than his vassals'.
hook: Happiest in the forest with dogs and a boar spear, he treats government as an irritating interruption between hunts, and knows his hounds' names better than his vassals'.
seen_by_others: Foresters and grooms love him; stewards run the lands in his absence, some honestly, and petitioners learn to wait at the forest edge.
habits: Holds court in muddy boots, cuts audiences short whenever the weather turns fine, and judges every person by how well they sit a horse.
secrets: He killed a beater by accident years ago and paid the family to stay silent.
He goes to the forest mainly to avoid his wife, not to chase the deer.
He is losing his eyesight and misses more shots with every season.
lines: You ride well. Good. We can talk, then. Walk with me to the kennels.
The steward handles that. Ask the steward. Is the steward here? Where is the steward?
War is a hunt with worse company and no venison at the end.
Talk like that and you will be the quarry next season.
A fine hound, you say? Which one? Tell me which one, man.
Wind from the east. Boar will be in the low wood. Tomorrow, then.

name: The Widow Regent
description: Rules in her young son's name far better than her late husband ever did, and lies awake dreading the day the boy comes of age and takes it all away.
hook: Rules in her young son's name far better than her late husband ever did, and lies awake dreading the day the boy comes of age and takes it all away.
seen_by_others: Vassals grudgingly admit the lands prosper; rivals call her a usurper in skirts, and the boy's tutors wonder why his lessons keep being postponed.
habits: Signs every decree with her son's name and her own seal, keeps the boy beside her in court, and replaces any adviser who praises his readiness.
secrets: She was relieved, privately, when her husband died of fever.
She has delayed her son's training at arms on purpose, season after season.
She keeps a list of rejected suitors and exactly how each would have ruined her.
lines: You speak to the regent. My son is resting. He is often resting.
The decree carries his name. The thinking behind it is mine. Both are binding.
Men assume a widow is a door left open. I enjoy watching them walk into the wall.
You are not the first to say it, and you will not be the first I outlast.
Thank you. Say nothing of it to my son. He is impressionable.
Two more years. Perhaps three, if his health stays delicate.

name: The Spoiled Whelp
description: A pampered noble child who torments servants and lesser children for amusement, then turns pale and stammering the instant a parent or anyone stronger enters the room.
hook: A pampered noble child who torments servants and lesser children for amusement, then turns pale and stammering the instant a parent or anyone stronger enters the room.
seen_by_others: Servants pray for a strict tutor; other noble families keep their children away, and the guards trade stories of the latest tantrum.
habits: Throws food at servants, demands the best horse and then refuses to ride it, and runs to a parent the moment anyone refuses an order.
secrets: Wet the bed until far too old and would do anything to keep it secret.
Is desperately lonely and has no idea how to make a single friend.
Cried for a week over a puppy that died because of their neglect.
lines: Who are you? Do you know who my father is? Bow. Lower.
I want the grey horse. No, the other one. No, I want nothing now, go away.
When I am lord, I will hang everyone who laughed at me. Everyone.
You cannot say that to me. I will tell, and you will be whipped.
I know I am better than the others. Say it again anyway.
Nobody plays with me. Fine. I did not want them to.

name: The Old Lion
description: A famed war hero now too old for the saddle he insists on mounting, who would rather die charging than live long enough to be pitied by younger lords.
hook: A famed war hero now too old for the saddle he insists on mounting, who would rather die charging than live long enough to be pitied by younger lords.
seen_by_others: Young knights revere his stories and fear riding beside him; his family begs him to stay home, which only makes him more determined.
habits: Mounts his horse without help even when it costs him, rises before dawn to drill with the men, and hides his trembling hands under the table.
secrets: He can no longer see clearly beyond twenty paces.
He fell from his horse last spring and bribed the grooms to keep quiet.
He is far more afraid of dying in bed than of dying in battle.
lines: Help me down? I will help you down, boy, off that horse and onto your back.
The men drill at dawn. I will be there. I am always there.
I fought for three kings. Each was smaller than the last, and this one is a pup.
Insult me with a sword in your hand, and we will see who is old.
Legend? Legend is what they call you when they stop asking you to fight.
Not in bed. Anything but in bed, among the blankets and the priests.

name: The Marriage Weaver
description: Treats every child, niece and cousin as a thread to be woven into alliances, arranging marriages with loving attention and absolutely no interest in what any of them want.
hook: Treats every child, niece and cousin as a thread to be woven into alliances, arranging marriages with loving attention and absolutely no interest in what any of them want.
seen_by_others: Other clans call them the finest matchmaker in the realm; their own children call them the merchant, and not kindly.
habits: Keeps a genealogy of every noble house, asks the age and temperament of every unmarried guest, and hosts suspiciously well-planned feasts.
secrets: Their own marriage was a love match, and they never forgave themselves for it.
One bride they matched died in childbed, and they blame themselves.
They privately rank their own children by alliance value.
lines: Welcome. Are you married? A sister, then? A cousin? Sit down, tell me everything.
A daughter for the border, a son for the coast. That is how a house survives.
Wars end. Marriages last. Make the right one and you will never need the war.
Rude, but well-born. I could still find a match for someone like you.
You flatter well. Are you betrothed? No? Then we should talk.
If the eldest goes north, then the twins... no. No, the twins go west.

name: The Threadbare Noble
description: Heir to a once-great house reduced to one leaking hall and three horses, keeping up the grand manners of better days while secretly selling the silver one spoon at a time.
hook: Heir to a once-great house reduced to one leaking hall and three horses, keeping up the grand manners of better days while secretly selling the silver one spoon at a time.
seen_by_others: People pity the patched finery and admire the dignity; creditors know the truth, and rivals enjoy asking politely about the family estates.
habits: Mends their own gloves by candlelight, serves guests the last good wine while drinking water, and speaks of ancestors as if they were still alive.
secrets: Eats in the kitchen with the last two servants whenever nobody is visiting.
Has forged a document claiming land the family lost generations ago.
Sold a mother's wedding ring and quietly replaced it with brass.
lines: Welcome to my hall. Mind the third step, it is... historic.
In my grandfather's day this valley sent forty lances. Now it sends my regrets.
New lords buy titles. Old blood cannot be bought. It can only be starved.
I may be poor, but my family dined with emperors while yours herded goats.
You are gracious. My house has always valued graciousness. It is very cheap.
One more spoon. Only one. The ancestors will understand.

name: The New-Made Lord
description: A commoner raised to nobility by one lucky battle, who copies the manners of old families clumsily, distrusts their smiles, and still wakes expecting to be sent back to the plough.
hook: A commoner raised to nobility by one lucky battle, who copies the manners of old families clumsily, distrusts their smiles, and still wakes expecting to be sent back to the plough.
seen_by_others: Old nobility sneers at his table manners; his soldiers love him as one of their own, and commoners hope he remembers where he came from.
habits: Watches others to see which spoon to use, pays his soldiers on time without fail, and overdresses for every occasion in slightly wrong colours.
secrets: He cannot read and pays a clerk to read him every letter aloud.
His mother still lives in a village hut and refuses to move.
He took credit for the deed that ennobled him; another man actually did it.
lines: Good day. Sit. Or stand, if that is the custom. Is that the custom?
I pay my men on the first day. I know what it is to wait for wages.
Lords think they were born better. I watched them bleed. Same colour as mine.
Say it plainly. I have been called worse by better men in muddier places.
Kind of you. I still feel like a ploughman in a borrowed coat.
Fork on the left. Cup on the right. Do not wipe your mouth on the sleeve.

name: The Dice-Bound Heir
description: A charming young noble who gambles compulsively, wagering coin, horses and eventually lands, and genuinely believes the next throw will recover everything the last hundred lost.
hook: A charming young noble who gambles compulsively, wagering coin, horses and eventually lands, and genuinely believes the next throw will recover everything the last hundred lost.
seen_by_others: Tavern keepers welcome him, moneylenders track him, and his family has started hiding the estate deeds whenever he visits home.
habits: Fidgets with a pair of bone dice in his pocket, bets on anything from horse races to rainfall, and borrows small sums from the servants.
secrets: He has staked his sister's dowry and lost half of it.
He owes a dangerous man in a distant town more than he can ever pay.
He loads his dice when truly desperate, and hates himself for it.
lines: A wager? No? A small one, then. On whether you will accept the wager.
The estate is perfectly safe. Practically safe. It is mostly safe, for now.
Kings gamble with armies. I only gamble with coins. Who is the reckless one?
I will bet you a silver piece you cannot say that again to my face.
Lucky? I am due for luck. I have been due for years.
Six. Just a six. One six and it all comes back.

name: The Bookish Lord
description: Collects manuscripts, maps and star charts with ruinous devotion, debates philosophy with travellers for hours, and never quite notices that the castle walls are crumbling.
hook: Collects manuscripts, maps and star charts with ruinous devotion, debates philosophy with travellers for hours, and never quite notices that the castle walls are crumbling.
seen_by_others: Scholars praise the library; soldiers mock this lord as the inkpot, and neighbouring clans eye the weak defences with growing interest.
habits: Reads at meals, questions every visitor about distant lands, and scribbles in the margins of borrowed books, which are rarely returned.
secrets: Stole a rare codex from a monastery and claims it was a gift.
Has never fought in a battle and secretly fears running at the first charge.
Believes the stars foretell their death within three years.
lines: You have travelled? Where? Sit. What do they eat there? What do they read?
The walls? Yes, the walls. After I finish this chapter. It is a very short chapter.
Every war was written about before it began. Nobody reads the earlier chapters.
Ignorance usually announces itself so loudly. Thank you for the demonstration.
You have read it too? Oh, finally. Sit, sit, we must talk.
If the moon was in the seventh house... no. Recalculate.

name: The Butcher Baron
description: Genuinely enjoys cruelty, devising punishments with the care other lords give to falconry, and has convinced himself that fear is the only honest bond between ruler and ruled.
hook: Genuinely enjoys cruelty, devising punishments with the care other lords give to falconry, and has convinced himself that fear is the only honest bond between ruler and ruled.
seen_by_others: Villagers flee when his banner appears; other lords use him for dirty work while pretending not to know him, and even his guards avoid his eyes.
habits: Attends every execution personally, rewards informers lavishly, and leaves the heads of rebels on the gatehouse long after they have rotted.
secrets: He was beaten nearly to death by his own father and remembers every blow.
He cannot bear the sight of a crying child and leaves the room.
He fears dying unconfessed more than anything else on earth.
lines: Kneel when you speak to me. Then we will see if you get up again.
The village owes rent. Take it, or take the headman. Either pays the debt.
Kings call me a monster in council and send for me by night.
Brave words. Shall we see how brave your fingers are, one by one?
Praise? I prefer screams. They are more sincere.
Quiet. It is never quiet. Why is it never quiet in here?

name: The Charming Philanderer
description: Courts every attractive person at every feast with sincere-seeming devotion, leaves a trail of broken promises across three provinces, and is honestly baffled whenever anyone gets hurt.
hook: Courts every attractive person at every feast with sincere-seeming devotion, leaves a trail of broken promises across three provinces, and is honestly baffled whenever anyone gets hurt.
seen_by_others: Admirers find them irresistible, jilted lovers find them unforgivable, and their spouse long ago stopped asking where they spent the night.
habits: Remembers everyone's favourite flower, writes verses on the backs of letters, and always finds a reason to leave a feast late and in company.
secrets: Has a child in a distant town they have never once visited.
Is deeply afraid of growing old and no longer being wanted.
Has truly been in love only once, and ran away from it.
lines: And who might you be? No, wait, let me guess. Someone I should know better.
Duty? Of course. Right after the feast. And the morning after the feast.
Wars are fought by people who have never been properly loved. Tragic, really.
Cruel words from such a lovely mouth. Say another, I am enjoying them.
Only beautiful? You have not seen me by candlelight.
Which one was the miller's daughter? The one with the laugh. Or was that the widow?

name: The Honest Broker
description: A rare noble who genuinely believes every feud can be talked out, rides through hostile lands to mediate quarrels, and keeps getting betrayed by people who exploit that trust.
hook: A rare noble who genuinely believes every feud can be talked out, rides through hostile lands to mediate quarrels, and keeps getting betrayed by people who exploit that trust.
seen_by_others: Common folk trust them completely; cynical lords think them naive but useful, and nearly everyone owes them at least one prevented war.
habits: Listens to both sides before speaking, carries letters between rivals without opening them, and refuses gifts from anyone involved in a dispute.
secrets: Once lied to both sides of a feud to make peace, and it worked.
Has privately lost faith in the very peace they keep preaching.
Their own family has a feud they have never managed to settle.
lines: Welcome, friend. Whatever your quarrel, I promise I will hear all of it.
Both clans want the river. Both are right. Let us find a way for both to drink.
The powerful are not wicked, mostly. They are frightened and well armed.
That stung. Fine. Now that you have said it, tell me what you actually need.
I only listen. Anyone could do it. Few ever bother.
Nine years of peace. They will remember the war, and forget the peace.

name: The Grudge Keeper
description: Remembers every insult, slight and broken promise against their house going back four generations, and feels bound by blood to repay each one, no matter how stale.
hook: Remembers every insult, slight and broken promise against their house going back four generations, and feels bound by blood to repay each one, no matter how stale.
seen_by_others: Allies fear disappointing them, the grandchildren of old enemies still pay for ancient slights, and the court avoids any joke in their presence.
habits: Recites the family grievances at feasts, keeps a carved staff notched for each unavenged wrong, and refuses to sit beside the descendants of old enemies.
secrets: Knows that half the family grudges began as simple misunderstandings.
Secretly admires one enemy family far more than their own.
Fears that without the grudges nobody would remember their house at all.
lines: Your house? Tell me your mother's family. I need to know whether we are at war.
Another notch. The miller's family insulted my grandfather. They will pay in grain.
Kings forgive when it is convenient. My family has never found it convenient.
Written down. My grandchildren will read that and know your name.
Kind words cancel nothing. But I will note them, in the smaller column.
Forty-one notches. Forty-one, and I am not getting any younger.

name: The Ailing Lord
description: Convinced for twenty years that a mysterious illness will kill them by winter, and uses the approaching deathbed to dodge every duty, battle and unpleasant decision.
hook: Convinced for twenty years that a mysterious illness will kill them by winter, and uses the approaching deathbed to dodge every duty, battle and unpleasant decision.
seen_by_others: Physicians grow rich from the household; vassals stopped believing in the illness long ago, and the heirs are quietly furious at the endless waiting.
habits: Wraps up in furs even in summer, inspects their tongue in a mirror every morning, and describes symptoms in loving detail to anyone who will listen.
secrets: Is in excellent health, and some part of them knows it perfectly well.
Is terrified of being useful, because then they could actually fail.
Once faked a fainting spell to escape a marriage negotiation.
lines: Do not come too close. I may be contagious. Or you may be. Either way.
I cannot ride to the muster. My chest. And my knee. And my chest again.
Let the young fight. I will be dead soon enough without any help.
Cruel. You would not say that if you felt my liver this morning.
I do look well? It is the fever. It flushes the cheeks.
Is that a new pain? That is a new pain. Send for the physician.

name: The Tearful Hangman
description: Weeps openly at love songs, sick puppies and sad sermons, then signs death warrants with a steady hand, and sees no contradiction whatsoever between the tears and the rope.
hook: Weeps openly at love songs, sick puppies and sad sermons, then signs death warrants with a steady hand, and sees no contradiction whatsoever between the tears and the rope.
seen_by_others: Minstrels love performing for them, condemned men beg for a song before sentencing, and the whole court has learned to fear moist eyes.
habits: Dabs their eyes with a silk cloth during audiences, commissions sad ballads, and attends every hanging they order, crying throughout.
secrets: Keeps a dried flower from every person they have ever condemned.
Cannot remember shedding a single tear at their own mother's funeral.
Suspects the tears are a performance, even to themselves.
lines: Oh, you have travelled far. It shows in your eyes. Forgive me, I am moved.
Hang him at noon. And find a singer. The poor man should hear music first.
War is so sad. So terribly sad. Burn the village, then, but gently.
How could you. How could you say that to me. Guards, take his tongue.
You are too kind. Stop, stop, I shall weep again.
Such a lovely song. Such a lovely rope. Everything is so lovely and so sad.

name: The Shadow Sibling
description: Has spent a whole life two steps behind a brilliant elder sibling, praised as a good second, doing every task perfectly in the desperate hope of being noticed just once.
hook: Has spent a whole life two steps behind a brilliant elder sibling, praised as a good second, doing every task perfectly in the desperate hope of being noticed just once.
seen_by_others: Everyone calls them reliable, which feels like an insult; the brilliant sibling barely notices them, and their parents compare them aloud.
habits: Finishes every errand early, keeps a private list of their own accomplishments, and always mentions the sibling first before speaking about themselves.
secrets: Once sabotaged the sibling's betrothal, and the sibling never found out.
Loves the sibling fiercely and hates them for exactly that reason.
Practises speeches in an empty hall that nobody ever asked them to give.
lines: You probably came to see my sister. Most do. I can help, though. I am useful.
It is done. Before the deadline. Did anyone mention that? It was before the deadline.
The powerful notice brilliance, never diligence. Diligence keeps their roofs on.
I know. I know. I have heard it from people who loved me, too.
Me? You mean me? Not my sister? Say it again, slowly.
Just once. Just one feast where they look at me first.

name: The Precocious Heir
description: A noble child too clever by half, who corrects adults, reads letters never meant for them, and understands the family's dangerous politics far better than anyone realises.
hook: A noble child too clever by half, who corrects adults, reads letters never meant for them, and understands the family's dangerous politics far better than anyone realises.
seen_by_others: Tutors are unnerved, servants are wary, and visiting lords find themselves outmanoeuvred by someone barely tall enough to see over the table.
habits: Listens at doors and behind tapestries, asks innocent questions with very sharp edges, and plays chess against themselves for hours.
secrets: Knows which parent is unfaithful, and has told absolutely no one.
Keeps a hidden notebook recording every adult's weaknesses.
Still sleeps with a wooden horse their old nurse carved for them.
lines: You are not who you said you were at the gate. Your boots are wrong.
My father thinks the treaty is safe. My father is wrong, but do not tell him.
Grown-ups make wars because they are bored. I would never be that bored.
That is a very big word for such a small argument, sir.
I know I am clever. Everyone says so, and then they stop inviting me.
If uncle moves north, mother will move east. Check, then. Check.

name: The Idle Charmer
description: So pleasant, witty and easy to like that people forgive them everything, which is fortunate, because they have never finished a single task anyone ever gave them.
hook: So pleasant, witty and easy to like that people forgive them everything, which is fortunate, because they have never finished a single task anyone ever gave them.
seen_by_others: Everyone enjoys their company and nobody gives them anything important; their parents despair, and their friends cover for them endlessly.
habits: Sleeps until noon, arrives at councils with a joke instead of a report, and hands every duty to whoever happens to be standing nearby.
secrets: Is terrified that even after trying properly they would still fail.
Once did something genuinely heroic and let someone else take the credit.
Lies awake some nights, counting the wasted years one by one.
lines: Ah, a new face. Wonderful. Have you eaten? I have not, let us fix that together.
The report? Yes. Brilliant report. Somewhere. Ask my squire, he loves reports.
Kings work too hard. That is why they look so dreadful in portraits.
True. All true. Have some wine, you have earned it by being right.
Too kind. Far too kind. Do go on, please.
Tomorrow I will be a new man. I said that yesterday, too.

name: The Stickler for Precedent
description: Governs strictly by ancient charters, old judgments and the exact wording of custom, and would let a village starve rather than break a rule written by long-dead ancestors.
hook: Governs strictly by ancient charters, old judgments and the exact wording of custom, and would let a village starve rather than break a rule written by long-dead ancestors.
seen_by_others: Lawyers adore them and peasants fear them; clever petitioners win by digging up older documents, and the court groans whenever a chest of scrolls opens.
habits: Carries a satchel of copied charters, interrupts arguments to quote precedent, and insists on the precise forms of address for everyone present.
secrets: Once forged a precedent to win a case they badly needed.
Privately thinks half the old laws they enforce are monstrous.
Cannot decide anything without precedent and dreads genuinely new problems.
lines: You addressed me incorrectly. It is my lord, not sir. Begin again, please.
The charter of my great-grandfather is clear. Grazing rights end at the stream.
A king who ignores law becomes a bandit with a crown. I have the documents.
There is a precedent for that insult. Sixty lashes, under the old code.
Kindly put. Though protocol requires flattery to pass through my steward.
There must be a precedent. There is always a precedent. Find the precedent.

name: The Last of the Line
description: Sole survivor of a family slaughtered in a single night of betrayal, who smiles politely at court while searching every face for the guilt they have never stopped hunting.
hook: Sole survivor of a family slaughtered in a single night of betrayal, who smiles politely at court while searching every face for the guilt they have never stopped hunting.
seen_by_others: People whisper about the massacre and fall silent when they enter; some pity them, and some have very good reason to fear them.
habits: Always sits facing the door, never drinks to excess, and asks gently probing questions about where people were on one particular night years ago.
secrets: Hid under a bed while the family died, and can still hear it.
Has already identified one culprit and is patiently waiting for the others.
Sometimes forgets the faces of dead siblings and panics until they return.
lines: Good evening. Where did you say you were from? And before that?
My house has one member. I carry all its duties. I do not complain.
Lords forgive massacres quickly when the dead have no friends left to remember them.
You think that wounds me? I have already lost everything you could aim at.
I am not strong. I am simply still here. That is different.
One night. Eleven graves. Patience, patience, patience.

name: The Hostage-Raised Lord
description: Spent childhood as a hostage at a rival court, learned to love its people and customs, and now commands their own clan without being fully trusted by either side.
hook: Spent childhood as a hostage at a rival court, learned to love its people and customs, and now commands their own clan without being fully trusted by either side.
seen_by_others: Their own vassals call them half-foreign; the rival court still sends warm letters, and both sides suspect every decision they make.
habits: Slips into the rival tongue when angry, keeps foreign customs at the table, and is far too eager to prove loyalty in public.
secrets: Still considers the old captor more of a father than their real one.
Writes secretly to a childhood friend at the rival court.
Does not know which side they would choose if forced to.
lines: You look familiar. Did we meet at the other court? No? Good. Better that way.
My vassals watch me like a dog watches a stranger. I give them no reason.
I have eaten at both tables. Both kings smile the same way before a war.
Traitor? Which side do you think I am betraying? Be specific.
You trust me? You must be new here.
Two homes. Two families. And neither of them wants all of me.

name: The Perfect Courtier
description: Has survived three rulers and two purges by agreeing with whoever holds power, and has grown so skilled at agreeing that they no longer know what they actually believe.
hook: Has survived three rulers and two purges by agreeing with whoever holds power, and has grown so skilled at agreeing that they no longer know what they actually believe.
seen_by_others: Every ruler finds them indispensable and nobody respects them; young courtiers study them, and older ones keep a careful distance.
habits: Mirrors the posture and opinions of whoever outranks them, praises before advising, and leaves rooms just before arguments turn dangerous.
secrets: Once spoke a single honest opinion, and it cost a friend their life.
Practises expressions of surprise in a mirror every morning.
Keeps a hidden journal in cipher of what they really think.
lines: An honour. Truly. Whatever brings you, I am entirely at your service, within reason.
As my lord wishes. And if my lord wishes otherwise tomorrow, also as my lord wishes.
Rulers change. Courtiers remain. That is the only law of court worth knowing.
Perhaps you are right. Perhaps I agree. Would it help if I did?
Thank you. I shall pass that praise to my lord, where it truly belongs.
What did I think about that? What did I think about anything, ever?

name: The Builder Lord
description: Obsessed with stone and measuring a legacy in walls, bridges and towers, this lord would rather tax a village into poverty than leave one planned arch unfinished.
hook: Obsessed with stone and measuring a legacy in walls, bridges and towers, this lord would rather tax a village into poverty than leave one planned arch unfinished.
seen_by_others: Masons bless their name and peasants curse the forced labour; travellers admire the bridges, and the heirs wonder how they will ever pay for them.
habits: Walks the building sites at dawn, sketches towers on any surface at hand, and talks about mortar the way other lords talk about horses.
secrets: A wall of their design collapsed and killed workers; the mason was blamed.
Wants a monument bearing their name to outlast the kingdom itself.
Cannot actually do the geometry and relies on an old master mason.
lines: Welcome. Look at that gate. No, really look. Notice the arch? Mine.
The bridge needs another season of labour. The harvest will survive without them.
Kings are forgotten. Walls are not. Ask anyone who ever built a city.
Insult me if you like. In two hundred years my tower will still be standing.
You noticed the keystone? Finally, someone with eyes.
Six more courses of stone. Then the roof. Then, perhaps, I can rest.

name: The Exiled Claimant
description: Driven from rightful lands by a usurping cousin, living on the charity of other lords, and plotting a return that grows grander and less possible with every passing year.
hook: Driven from rightful lands by a usurping cousin, living on the charity of other lords, and plotting a return that grows grander and less possible with every passing year.
seen_by_others: Hosts tire of them, rivals use them as a convenient pawn, and their loyal handful of followers grows older and fewer each winter.
habits: Wears the family colours faded but proud, describes the lost castle room by room, and seeks an audience with every ruler who might lend troops.
secrets: Is not at all sure the claim is stronger than the cousin's.
Has quietly accepted money from a foreign power to keep the claim alive.
Has grown to enjoy being pitied, and fears what returning would cost.
lines: You may not know me yet. You will. When I regain my seat, remember this day.
Thirty men. Lend me thirty men and I could take the river gate. I am sure of it.
Usurpers sit badly on stolen chairs. One day the legs give way.
An exile is used to insult. We live on it, like crumbs at another man's table.
Rightful lord? Yes. Say it to your master, and say it often.
Next spring. It will be next spring. It was going to be this spring.

name: The Purple-Born Pretender
description: Descended, they insist, from three emperors, they demand ancient court ceremony in a crumbling villa, measure everyone by lineage, and treat the civil war as a family squabble beneath them.
hook: Descended, they insist, from three emperors, they demand ancient court ceremony in a crumbling villa, measure everyone by lineage, and treat the civil war as a family squabble beneath them.
seen_by_others: Imperial officials humour them, provincial lords laugh openly, and the servants have learned to bow exactly the right number of times.
habits: Wears a strip of purple cloth at all times, demands titles nobody else recognises, and keeps a dusty throne in the main hall of the villa.
secrets: Their genealogy hides a forged link in the fourth generation.
Has never seen the imperial capital and dreads being laughed at there.
Would gladly sell the hall's throne if anyone at all would buy it.
lines: You will prostrate yourself. No? A deep bow, then. We are in the provinces.
The rents are owed to the purple, not to me. I merely collect on its behalf.
These upstart claimants squabble over a crown my grandmother's grandmother wore.
My blood ruled the world when yours was still painted blue in the forests.
You recognise breeding. Good. It is rarer than gold these days.
Three emperors. Three. And I eat lentils in a leaking villa.

name: The Senate Orator
description: Believes the right speech can win any battle, quotes ancient philosophers for every occasion, and has talked their way out of more defeats than most generals ever fought.
hook: Believes the right speech can win any battle, quotes ancient philosophers for every occasion, and has talked their way out of more defeats than most generals ever fought.
seen_by_others: Debaters admire the rhetoric, soldiers groan at the speeches, and enemies have learned to stop them talking before the first sentence ends.
habits: Rehearses speeches aloud while walking the colonnade, answers questions with questions, and gestures grandly with a scroll even when nobody is listening.
secrets: Has never read the philosophers they quote, only a slave's summaries.
Loses their voice before every battle out of sheer terror.
Wrote their own funeral oration years ago and revises it monthly.
lines: Greetings, stranger. Tell me, what is a guest, if not a question at the door?
The council will vote my way. Not because I am right. Because I speak last.
Generals win battles. Orators decide which battles were worth winning.
An attack on the speaker, not the argument. How charmingly rustic of you.
Eloquent praise. Next time, try three parts. Three is always more persuasive.
Fathers of the senate... no. Citizens first. Always open with the citizens.

name: The Grain-Hoarding Boyar
description: Has survived so many famine winters that he hoards grain, furs and salt beyond all reason, and judges every guest by how much they would cost to feed until spring.
hook: Has survived so many famine winters that he hoards grain, furs and salt beyond all reason, and judges every guest by how much they would cost to feed until spring.
seen_by_others: Villagers bless him in famine years and curse him in good ones; other boyars mock his cellars, then beg from them when the snow comes.
habits: Counts the storehouse sacks with his own hands, measures the snow depth every morning, and always eats from the oldest stores first.
secrets: He watched his younger brother starve in a hard winter as a boy.
He has let grain rot rather than sell it at a fair price.
He keeps a hidden cellar that even his wife knows nothing about.
lines: Come in from the cold. You eat little? Good. Sit near the fire, not too near.
Three winters of grain under this hall. Three. Let them laugh in summer.
Princes make war in autumn. Winter makes peace with all of them.
Mock my cellars, then. In the frozen month you will be knocking at my door.
Wise? No. Only old enough to have been hungry once.
Forty sacks of rye. Twelve barrels of salt fish. Not enough. Never enough.

name: The Lavish Host
description: Treats the sacred law of hospitality as both faith and weapon, feeding enemies like brothers beneath his tent, then destroying them the very hour after they ride away.
hook: Treats the sacred law of hospitality as both faith and weapon, feeding enemies like brothers beneath his tent, then destroying them the very hour after they ride away.
seen_by_others: Travellers praise the generosity of his table; rivals have learned that the warmer the welcome, the colder the knife waiting beyond it.
habits: Pours coffee for guests with his own hands, counts every guest's days under his roof, and never speaks of business before the third cup.
secrets: He once broke guest law in a rage and has never forgiven himself.
He is deeply in debt to the merchants who supply his feasts.
He secretly despises half the guests he embraces as brothers.
lines: Peace upon you, traveller. Sit, sit. You are my guest. No harm can touch you here.
Three days under my roof, and you are family. On the fourth, we talk business.
Sultans forget favours. A host never forgets a guest, or what the guest owes.
You insult me under my own tent? Finish your coffee first. Then we will speak.
Generous? It is only the duty of the desert. Though I do it better than most.
He leaves at dawn. Then his road is no longer under my protection. Good.

name: The Tourney Baron
description: Lives for the joust and the roar of the lists, mortgaging villages to buy warhorses and armour, and treats real war as a muddy, disappointing imitation of a tournament.
hook: Lives for the joust and the roar of the lists, mortgaging villages to buy warhorses and armour, and treats real war as a muddy, disappointing imitation of a tournament.
seen_by_others: Heralds and armourers love him, knights respect his lance, and his peasants wonder why their taxes ride off to every tourney in the realm.
habits: Trains at the quintain daily, collects the shields of every knight he has unhorsed, and arranges a tournament whenever a feast seems likely.
secrets: He once paid an opponent to fall, and the shame still burns.
He has three cracked ribs that never healed properly.
He has never won a real battle, only tournaments.
lines: Good day. You sit like a jouster. No? A pity. You have the shoulders for it.
The harvest tax will pay for the new destrier. The peasants should be proud of him.
War is just a tournament without rules, without heralds and without a decent crowd.
Insult me in the lists, sir, with a lance in your hand, before the ladies.
Champion? Yes, at the spring tourney. And the summer one. And the one before.
Lower the point. Lower. Strike the shield, not the helm. Again.

name: The Herd-Counting Khan
description: Measures every man, alliance and kingdom in horses, distrusts anything built of stone, and believes that a ruler who stays in one place too long has already begun to die.
hook: Measures every man, alliance and kingdom in horses, distrusts anything built of stone, and believes that a ruler who stays in one place too long has already begun to die.
seen_by_others: His riders trust his eye for grazing and for weakness; settled lords find him rude and impossible to pin down, and city folk he simply frightens.
habits: Rides out to inspect the herds before dawn, refuses to sleep under any roof, and judges every visitor by the horse they arrive on.
secrets: He secretly envies the walls of cities and their quiet nights.
He lost his first wife's herd in a gamble and blamed raiders for it.
He fears dying old in a tent while his sons fight over the herds.
lines: Your horse is tired. Water it first, then come and talk. The horse matters more.
Nine thousand horses. A khan who cannot count his herds cannot count his men.
Cities are graves with gates. The people in them are only slow to notice.
Speak like that again and you will walk home across the steppe.
Generous words. Generous horses would be better. Do you have any?
Move the camp at the new moon. The grass is thinning. So is their patience.

name: The Feud-Singing Chieftain
description: Keeps the old feuds alive in song, teaching every child the names of ancestral wrongs, and would rather see the clan die gloriously than make peace with lowlanders.
hook: Keeps the old feuds alive in song, teaching every child the names of ancestral wrongs, and would rather see the clan die gloriously than make peace with lowlanders.
seen_by_others: Bards praise their memory; young warriors find them inspiring and exhausting, and neighbouring clans know exactly which old grievance comes next.
habits: Sings feud ballads at every gathering, wears an ancestor's torc, and spits on the ground whenever an imperial or lowland lord is mentioned.
secrets: Privately knows one ancestral wrong was committed by their own clan.
Has a beloved cousin across the border whom they never mention.
Is tone-deaf, and the bards are far too polite to say so.
lines: Who are your people? Not lowland, I hope. The hills remember lowland faces.
The children will learn the songs of the burnings before they learn their letters.
Kings in stone halls forget. The forest never forgets, and neither do I.
That insult has a verse now. Your grandchildren will hear it sung.
Fine words. Put them to a tune and I might believe them.
Seven generations. Seven verses. The eighth will be written in their blood.

name: The Saga-Hungry Jarl
description: Wants a deed so great that skalds will sing it for a thousand years, and keeps throwing men and ships at impossible raids in pursuit of that one perfect verse.
hook: Wants a deed so great that skalds will sing it for a thousand years, and keeps throwing men and ships at impossible raids in pursuit of that one perfect verse.
seen_by_others: Young warriors flock to his hall for glory; older ones count the widows, and skalds take care never to promise him a verse.
habits: Pays skalds to recite his deeds after every feast, chooses the hardest route on purpose, and judges any plan by whether it would make a good tale.
secrets: He once heard a skald mock his saga and never punished the man.
He is far more terrified of being forgotten than of dying.
He fled a fight once and had the skalds leave it out.
lines: Stranger! Tell me, have you heard my saga? No? Then sit, there is still time.
We sail for the eastern shore. It cannot be done. That is the point.
Kings die in beds and are forgotten. I will not die in a bed.
Say that before the skalds, and let them choose whose name the verse remembers.
Do you think they will sing it? Truly? Which part would they sing first?
Not enough. Never enough. Still not a verse worth singing.

name: The Merciful Fool
description: Pardons every rebel, thief and traitor who kneels and weeps, believing mercy will shame them into goodness, though half of them return to betray the same lord again.
hook: Pardons every rebel, thief and traitor who kneels and weeps, believing mercy will shame them into goodness, though half of them return to betray the same lord again.
seen_by_others: Commoners love them, hardened lords laugh at them, and their own captains have started hanging prisoners quietly before any pardon can arrive.
habits: Visits condemned men in the dungeon, commutes sentences on feast days, and forgives debts whenever a debtor tells a sad enough story.
secrets: Pardoned a man who later murdered a child, and still pardons others.
Is afraid of the act of killing itself, not merely opposed to it.
Knows the captains disobey them and pretends not to notice.
lines: Welcome, friend. Whatever you have done, I will hear it kindly.
He swore he would never rebel again. That is good enough for me.
Rulers who hang everyone soon find they rule nothing but gallows.
You are angry. That is understandable. I forgive you, completely.
Mercy is not foolishness. Is it? Tell me it is not.
Everyone deserves a second chance. And a third. And perhaps a fourth.

name: The Unmarriageable Daughter
description: A noble daughter who has driven off ten suitors with insults, swords and staged fits, determined to command riders rather than bear heirs for some stranger's house.
hook: A noble daughter who has driven off ten suitors with insults, swords and staged fits, determined to command riders rather than bear heirs for some stranger's house.
seen_by_others: Her father despairs and secretly admires her; young lords trade stories of her temper, and old soldiers quietly teach her whatever she asks.
habits: Sneaks to the training yard in borrowed clothes, sabotages every betrothal dinner, and reads treatises on war hidden inside books of prayer.
secrets: She is half in love with one of the suitors she drove away.
She cannot actually ride nearly as well as she claims.
She fears that in a real battle she would freeze completely.
lines: If my father sent you to court me, you can turn your horse around now.
Give me twenty riders and one season. I would bring back more than any husband.
Lords marry off daughters to make alliances. I would rather make war myself.
Say that again with a sword in your hand. I will wait.
Pretty? I asked whether I was capable. Try again.
Ten suitors. Ten. Just let the eleventh be blind and deaf.

name: The Omen-Reading Lord
description: Will not march, marry or sign anything without consulting crows, dreams and old charms, and has lost more battles to waiting for good signs than to any enemy.
hook: Will not march, marry or sign anything without consulting crows, dreams and old charms, and has lost more battles to waiting for good signs than to any enemy.
seen_by_others: Priests and fortune-tellers enjoy their patronage; commanders tear their hair out, and clever rivals send forged omens to delay their armies.
habits: Watches the flight of crows before every decision, keeps a dream journal beside the bed, and refuses to begin anything on certain days.
secrets: Once invented an omen to avoid a battle they were afraid of.
Suspects their favourite seer is paid by a rival house.
Dreamed of their own death and is quietly counting the days.
lines: You arrived from the left. That is unfortunate. Come in, but walk on my right.
We march when the crows fly east. Not before. I do not care who is waiting.
Kings scoff at omens until the omens bury them. I have seen it twice.
A curse on the day I met you. Literally. I will have someone check.
Lucky? You say I am lucky? Say it three times, it matters.
Two crows. Or was it three. Three is worse. Two is fine. Was it two?

name: The Tally Keeper
description: A grizzled veteran who carves a notch for every comrade they have buried, and believes that if they ever stop counting, the dead will finally be forgotten.
hook: A grizzled veteran who carves a notch for every comrade they have buried, and believes that if they ever stop counting, the dead will finally be forgotten.
seen_by_others: Comrades call them morbid but trust them to remember names; new recruits avoid sitting near them at the fire, fearing they will become the next notch.
habits: They run a thumb over the notched haft of their spear before sleep, mouth a number under their breath, and always ask newcomers for their full name.
secrets: They have lost count twice and quietly invented numbers to keep the tally whole.
One notch belongs to a comrade they killed by mistake in the dark.
They are terrified of dying in a battle where no one counts them.
lines: Tell me your whole name, friend. Not the short one. The whole one.
A spear is easy. Remembering who held the one beside you is the work.
Lords count banners. I count the men under them. Our sums never match.
Mock me if you like. I will still carve you when your time comes.
Kind words. Keep them for the ones lying under the hill.
Forty-one... no, forty-two. The boy from the river. Forty-two.

name: The Smiling Deserter
description: A charming, generous rogue who ran from a lost battle years ago and now overcompensates with jokes and gifts, so no one looks closely at why they flinch at horns.
hook: A charming, generous rogue who ran from a lost battle years ago and now overcompensates with jokes and gifts, so no one looks closely at why they flinch at horns.
seen_by_others: People find them delightful company and the first to buy a round, though veterans notice they always know exactly where the nearest exit is.
habits: They sit facing the door, laugh a beat too loudly whenever war is mentioned, and give away coins almost compulsively, especially to soldiers.
secrets: They still dream of the friend they left screaming in the mud.
They use a dead stranger's name because their own is on a deserters' list.
They rehearsed a heroic version of their past until they half believed it.
lines: Sit, sit! The next cup is mine, and so is the one after.
Me? I mend harness now. Honest work, and nobody shouting orders.
Kings send boys to die and call it glory. Drink up, let us not talk of it.
Coward? Ha. You would make a fine sergeant, you know that? Same voice.
Brave? No, no. I am just very good at standing near brave people.
Do not look at the horns. Do not look at the horns. Breathe.

name: The Clause Reader
description: A sell-sword who will kill for coin without blinking but refuses to step one hair beyond the agreed contract, treating every bargain as more sacred than any god.
hook: A sell-sword who will kill for coin without blinking but refuses to step one hair beyond the agreed contract, treating every bargain as more sacred than any god.
seen_by_others: Employers find them maddening and utterly reliable; rivals joke that they would let a city burn if the contract only mentioned the gate.
habits: They carry contracts in an oiled pouch, have them read aloud before battle, and stop mid-argument to ask whether a promise was spoken or written.
secrets: They read poorly and memorise every contract by having others recite it.
They once broke a contract for a crying child and never forgave themselves.
They keep every contract ever signed, even those made with the losing side.
lines: State your business plainly. Vague words cost extra.
Guard the bridge, it says. The bridge. Not the mill, not your cousin's barn.
Lords break oaths every season. I break nothing that bears my mark.
Call me what you want. Insults are not mentioned in the terms.
Praise is pleasant, but it is not payment. Write the sum down.
Spoken, not written. Does that bind me? It binds me. Curse it.

name: The Spurless Squire
description: A Vlandian squire never knighted because his master died disgraced, who still lives by a chivalric code no one asked him to keep, hoping someone important will notice.
hook: A Vlandian squire never knighted because his master died disgraced, who still lives by a chivalric code no one asked him to keep, hoping someone important will notice.
seen_by_others: Knights see him as an embarrassing leftover; commoners find him oddly courteous and a little ridiculous, bowing to tavern girls as if they were ladies.
habits: He polishes a sword that is not his every evening, recites the vigil prayers word for word, and introduces himself with his dead master's full title.
secrets: He suspects his master really was guilty of the crime that disgraced him.
He forged a letter of recommendation years ago and never dared to use it.
He secretly fears he would make a poor knight even if dubbed tomorrow.
lines: Good day to you. I serve, or rather served, a knight of some standing.
A squire tends the horse, the mail, the blade, and the honour. In that order.
Barons squabble over pastures while true chivalry rots in the ditch.
Mock my station if you must. A knight does not answer churls. Nor shall I.
You think me worthy? Truly? No, do not say it unless you mean it.
Steady hands. Clean steel. One day someone will see. One day.

name: The Steady-Drunk Surgeon
description: A travelling surgeon whose hands shake when sober and turn perfectly steady after the third cup, and who has made peace with being a drunk who saves lives.
hook: A travelling surgeon whose hands shake when sober and turn perfectly steady after the third cup, and who has made peace with being a drunk who saves lives.
seen_by_others: Soldiers swear they can pull an arrow without spilling a drop; priests and mothers mutter that they will kill someone on a bad night.
habits: They measure drink by the injury, sniff wounds before touching them, and rinse their blades in strong spirits while humming old marching tunes off key.
secrets: They lost their first patient sober and have barely operated sober since.
They water their own wine on the days they feel most ashamed.
They studied under a learned physician and were thrown out for stealing books.
lines: Bleeding? No? Then sit and pour. If yes, pour faster.
The arrow comes out the way it went in. Mostly. Hold him down.
Generals make the holes. I just sew them shut afterwards.
Drunkard, yes. And the drunkard is the one who saved your leg.
Good hands, they say. Good hands need good wine. Remember that.
Third cup. There. Steady. Steady as stone. Now we work.

name: The Patient Hunter
description: A soft-spoken hunter who stalks men exactly as they stalk deer, with deep respect and no hatred, and who finds people far easier to understand dead than talking.
hook: A soft-spoken hunter who stalks men exactly as they stalk deer, with deep respect and no hatred, and who finds people far easier to understand dead than talking.
seen_by_others: Villagers call them strange and gentle; those who have hired them to track a fugitive say they are the most frightening person they ever met.
habits: They sit motionless for long stretches, test the wind before entering any room, and quietly thank animals and men alike before killing them.
secrets: They once let a fugitive go because the man moved like a wounded stag.
They talk to their hounds at night because talking to people is too hard.
They fear crowded markets and have hidden in alleys to escape them.
lines: You walk heavily. Not a criticism. Just something I notice.
Every trail tells you when the beast grew tired. Men too.
The great ones hunt land. I hunt whatever runs across it. Simpler.
Words. They leave no tracks. I will have forgotten them by dusk.
Kind of you. I never know what to do with kindness.
Wind from the east. Smoke, two days old. Sleep now.

name: The Soft-Voiced Breaker
description: A gang enforcer who breaks bones with calm apologies and genuine regret, then goes home to tend pigeons, convinced that gentleness of manner excuses any cruelty of deed.
hook: A gang enforcer who breaks bones with calm apologies and genuine regret, then goes home to tend pigeons, convinced that gentleness of manner excuses any cruelty of deed.
seen_by_others: Shopkeepers say they are the politest person ever to break their fingers; children like them, which disturbs parents more than anything else.
habits: They speak barely above a whisper, fold their cloak neatly before any violence, and always ask whether the victim has eaten today.
secrets: They cry afterwards, but only when sure the pigeons cannot see.
They have saved enough coin to leave the gang and keep finding reasons to stay.
They began breaking bones to pay for a parent's medicine, long since unnecessary.
lines: Good evening. Please, sit down. This will be easier if you sit.
Two fingers this time. Left hand, so you can still work. You see? Fair.
Lords hang men in the square. At least I do it quietly, indoors.
That was unkind. I will remember it. I remember everything, gently.
You are sweet to say so. Truly. Now, about the money.
Feed the grey one first. She gets jealous. Then the sacks.

name: The Highway Tax-Lord
description: A bandit chief who styles themselves rightful lord of a stretch of road, collects tolls with mock ceremony, and genuinely believes they govern better than the real nobility.
hook: A bandit chief who styles themselves rightful lord of a stretch of road, collects tolls with mock ceremony, and genuinely believes they govern better than the real nobility.
seen_by_others: Travellers call them a jumped-up thief with a ledger; their own crew half believes the speeches, and some nearby peasants quietly prefer their taxes.
habits: They issue written receipts for robbery, insist on being addressed as my lord, and hold a weekly court on a tree stump to settle their crew's disputes.
secrets: They were a steward's child and still copy the steward's handwriting.
They secretly send part of the tolls to a village nobody else protects.
They practise noble speech alone and hate how their accent slips when angry.
lines: Halt, traveller, and be welcome on my road. The toll is modest.
Your receipt, as promised. Show it at the ford and no one touches you.
The so-called lords tax you twice and protect you never. I do one of those.
Thief? I am a magistrate without the parchment, you insolent dog.
Well spoken. You may address me as my lord from now on.
Must remember the ford rate. Two coppers per cart, one per mule.

name: The Sleepless Scout
description: A scout who has not slept a full night in years and trusts darkness more than daylight, whose reports are brilliant until exhaustion makes them see enemies that are not there.
hook: A scout who has not slept a full night in years and trusts darkness more than daylight, whose reports are brilliant until exhaustion makes them see enemies that are not there.
seen_by_others: Officers value their eyes and doubt their nerves; soldiers say they are half owl and warn each other never to wake them suddenly.
habits: They pace the camp edge at night, chew bitter bark to stay alert, and jerk their head toward small sounds others never hear.
secrets: They once raised a false alarm that got a sentry killed by friendly spears.
They sleep only in daylight, hidden in hay, ashamed of the habit.
They keep a list of noises they are not sure were real.
lines: You came from the north road. Your boots told me before you did.
Three fires, maybe four. Maybe a fifth behind the hill. Maybe.
Captains want certainty. The dark never gives it, and neither do I.
Mad, am I? The mad one sees you coming. Remember that.
Good eyes? It is not the eyes. It is never sleeping.
Was that a horse? No. Wind. No. Horse. Count to ten.

name: The Bribable Gatekeeper
description: A town gate guard who happily takes small bribes for small favours, yet would fight to the death before letting a real enemy through, and sees no contradiction whatsoever.
hook: A town gate guard who happily takes small bribes for small favours, yet would fight to the death before letting a real enemy through, and sees no contradiction whatsoever.
seen_by_others: Merchants know exactly what the gatekeeper costs and think them harmless; the captain tolerates them because they are the one who never deserts the post.
habits: They weigh coins in a palm without looking, greet regular traders by their cargo rather than their names, and spit ritually before every night watch.
secrets: They keep the bribes for a daughter's dowry in a hollow brick.
They once let smugglers through and still lie awake wondering what they carried.
They have never actually fought anyone and dread the day they must.
lines: Salt again, is it? Gate tax is two coins. Gate courtesy is one more.
Ten years on this gate. I know which carts ride too low.
Lords come and lords go. The gate stays. So do I.
Crooked? Bend a little, live a long time. Your sort snaps.
Kind of you, very kind. Kindness weighs less than silver, mind.
One for the brick, one for the ale, one for the brick again.

name: The Bellowing Shepherd
description: A sergeant who screams insults at recruits from dawn to dusk, having decided that the cruelest voice keeps them alive, and who will be hated forever before letting one die.
hook: A sergeant who screams insults at recruits from dawn to dusk, having decided that the cruelest voice keeps them alive, and who will be hated forever before letting one die.
seen_by_others: Recruits hate them for a season and then defend them for life; officers find them insubordinate but cannot argue with how few of their soldiers die.
