habits: They inspect every boot personally, never eat before the squad does, and lower their voice to a whisper only when someone is actually dying.
secrets: They keep copies of the letters their recruits send home, in case one is lost.
They wept openly at the first funeral they caused and swore never again.
They were the worst recruit in their own company once.
lines: You. Stand up straight before I decide you are furniture.
Shield higher. Higher! A shield at your belt is a shield for your corpse.
Commanders draw lines on maps. I count the boots that come back.
Say it again, louder. Good. Now put that anger into the drill.
Praise is for funerals, recruit. Get back in line.
Eleven out, eleven back. Eleven. Thank the heavens. Eleven.

name: The Song-Hungry Youth
description: A young soldier desperate to do one deed worthy of a song, who volunteers for every suicidal charge and keeps rewriting the verses that will someday be sung about them.
hook: A young soldier desperate to do one deed worthy of a song, who volunteers for every suicidal charge and keeps rewriting the verses that will someday be sung about them.
seen_by_others: Veterans call them a pup who will die stupidly; tavern regulars find them sweet; bards owe them drinks for all the ideas they hand out.
habits: They hum half-finished verses about themselves, polish armour they cannot afford, and ask every old soldier what the bravest thing they ever saw was.
secrets: They froze in their first skirmish and claim they were flanking.
They have written their own death song in case no one else does.
They secretly wish they had been born a bard instead.
lines: Have you heard of me yet? No? You will, give it a season.
I asked for the front rank. Again. The sergeant laughed. Again.
Great lords get songs for sitting on horses. I will earn mine on foot.
Laugh all you like. Nobody ever sings about the laughing ones.
You think it would make a good verse? Which part? Tell me which part!
And the young lion stood alone... no. And the bold one... no.

name: The Lucky Survivor
description: A soldier celebrated for surviving every massacre and revered as charmed, who knows the luck is really a talent for finding the right corpse to hide beneath.
hook: A soldier celebrated for surviving every massacre and revered as charmed, who knows the luck is really a talent for finding the right corpse to hide beneath.
seen_by_others: Soldiers touch their shoulder before battle for luck and fight to stand beside them; a few sharp-eyed sergeants suspect the truth and say nothing.
habits: They choose positions near ditches and wagons, smear themselves in mud before battle claiming superstition, and accept tribute for blessings with a solemn face.
secrets: They have played dead beneath friends who were still breathing.
They sell little luck charms and know every one is worthless.
They fear the day their reputation forces them into the front rank.
lines: Touch the shoulder, lad. Left one. That is where the luck lives.
Six battles. Six. Stay near me and keep your head low. Lower.
Every war, the same promises. Every war, I walk home. Draw your own conclusions.
Call me what you like. I will be drinking at your wake.
Charmed, yes. The gods favour me. Do not ask them why.
Ditch on the left. Wagon behind. Good ground to die near, not on.

name: The Penitent Blade
description: A mercenary who prays aloud for the soul of every man they kill, gives part of each wage to temples, and then signs on for the next bloody season anyway.
hook: A mercenary who prays aloud for the soul of every man they kill, gives part of each wage to temples, and then signs on for the next bloody season anyway.
seen_by_others: Comrades find the prayers eerie but comforting; priests take the coin while frowning, and enemies who hear the chanting across the field lose their nerve.
habits: They kneel briefly beside fallen enemies, mark their blade with ash after each fight, and fast the day before collecting their pay.
secrets: They suspect they pray only so the killing feels allowed.
They have never confessed their first killing, done long before soldiering.
They sometimes pick fights just to have something new to repent.
lines: Peace on you, stranger. May you never need my trade.
One blow, one prayer. I owe the heavens a very long list.
Princes buy pardons with gold. I pay mine in knees and ash.
Insult me. It is penance cheaply bought. Go on.
Do not praise a killer. Pray for one, if you must speak.
Forgive this one. And the one before. And the ones to come.

name: The Dice-Sworn
description: A sell-sword drowning in gambling debts who lets a pair of bone dice choose their employer, their road, and sometimes whether a prisoner lives, calling it fairness.
hook: A sell-sword drowning in gambling debts who lets a pair of bone dice choose their employer, their road, and sometimes whether a prisoner lives, calling it fairness.
seen_by_others: Gamblers adore them and creditors hunt them; companions refuse to stand nearby when the dice come out over anything important.
habits: They roll dice absently while others speak, kiss them before major decisions, and keep a tally of debts scratched inside their belt in tiny marks.
secrets: They use loaded dice for the decisions they truly care about.
They owe money to dangerous people in at least three towns.
They once rolled for their own life against a captor and won.
lines: Evening. Fancy a throw? Small stakes. Then larger. Then interesting.
Your coin or the other fellow's, I let the bones choose. Fairer than me.
Kings gamble with whole provinces and call it policy. I just admit it.
Snake eyes says I forgive you. Lucky for you, it nearly said otherwise.
Flattery is a bet, friend. What are you hoping to win?
Six owed to the tanner, nine to the miller. Roll for which comes first.

name: The Forest-Right Poacher
description: A poacher turned outlaw who believes the forest belongs to whoever feeds a child from it, and who hates noble hunting parties with a quiet, patient, inherited fury.
hook: A poacher turned outlaw who believes the forest belongs to whoever feeds a child from it, and who hates noble hunting parties with a quiet, patient, inherited fury.
seen_by_others: Villagers protect them and eat their venison; foresters want them hanged; nobles call them vermin while they sit close enough to hear.
habits: They move through woods without snapping a twig, leave meat on poor doorsteps before dawn, and spit whenever they hear a hunting horn.
secrets: Their father was hanged for a single hare, and they watched it happen.
They once stole a nobleman's prize hawk and still keep its feathers.
They sometimes take deer just to spite the lord, not to eat.
lines: Hungry? Do not ask where this came from. Just eat.
Snare low, cut quick, carry it out through the stream. Easy.
Their forest. Their deer. Their law. Our hungry children. Odd sums.
Call me thief. The lord's deer do not mind who eats them.
Kind words, but kindness never filled a pot. Venison does.
Horns on the ridge. Lords hunting. Let them sweat in their silks.

name: The Hanged Man's Widow
description: A widow who joined the outlaws after her husband was hanged for debt, and who now robs with cold, methodical calm, always asking victims whether they have children first.
hook: A widow who joined the outlaws after her husband was hanged for debt, and who now robs with cold, methodical calm, always asking victims whether they have children first.
seen_by_others: Her band respects her more than their chief; travellers remember her as the robber who handed back their bread and kept their boots.
habits: She wears her husband's belt cinched twice, asks every captive about their family before deciding anything, and sharpens her knife slowly while others argue.
secrets: She knows who denounced her husband and has spared that man twice.
She still sets out two bowls whenever she eats alone.
She is beginning to enjoy the fear she causes, and hates herself for it.
lines: Children at home? Answer quickly and answer truly.
Boots, purse, cloak. Keep the bread. Keep the shirt. Now walk.
Lords hang poor men for debts and then dine with moneylenders. I remember.
Say it again. Slowly. I want to remember your face.
Pretty words. My husband had those too. Look where they took him.
Two bowls. Stupid. Just one. Just one now.

name: The Chronicling Mercenary
description: A literate sell-sword who signs on mainly to witness history up close, scribbling notes during sieges, and privately disappointed that real battles never match the old chronicles.
hook: A literate sell-sword who signs on mainly to witness history up close, scribbling notes during sieges, and privately disappointed that real battles never match the old chronicles.
seen_by_others: Captains find them useful for letters and maps but suspect they care more about the story than the victory; soldiers beg to have their names written down.
habits: They write by firelight in a cramped hand, interrupt officers to ask for dates and exact numbers, and compare every battle to one they read about.
secrets: They invent grand speeches for commanders who said nothing memorable.
They hope to be remembered as a writer, never as a soldier.
They once missed an entire battle while arguing with a scribe.
lines: Where are you from, and when did you leave? Exact dates, please.
The pen and the spear both earn wages. Only one earns memory.
The old emperors fought cleverly. These ones charge and hope. Sad.
Insult me if you wish. At least I will spell your name correctly.
You liked my account? Which part? Did the siege read well?
Not grand enough. No one will read this. Add rain. Rain always helps.

name: The Camp Mother
description: A bandit leader who runs her crew like a strict household, cooking, mending, and scolding, and who can order a throat cut and a stew stirred in the same breath.
hook: A bandit leader who runs her crew like a strict household, cooking, mending, and scolding, and who can order a throat cut and a stew stirred in the same breath.
seen_by_others: Her men call her mother and fear her more than any lord; captives are baffled to be fed well and then sold without hesitation.
habits: She counts heads at every meal, slaps wrists for bad table manners, and keeps a wooden spoon tucked in her belt beside a long knife.
secrets: She lost a son to fever long ago and never speaks of him.
She keeps a small purse for each of her men in case one wants to leave.
She secretly envies the farm wives her crew robs.
lines: You look starved. Sit. Eat. Then we discuss your purse.
Raid at dawn, back by noon, nobody touches the drink before supper.
Lords feed their dogs better than their peasants. My boys eat first.
Mind that tongue in my camp or I will take it out with the spoon.
Sweet of you. Sweet still does not get you out of chores, though.
Nine bowls. Ten men. Who is missing? Who is missing?

name: The Listening Jailer
description: A jailer who collects the confessions, regrets, and last words of prisoners as a private treasure, and who has come to love the dungeon more than daylight.
hook: A jailer who collects the confessions, regrets, and last words of prisoners as a private treasure, and who has come to love the dungeon more than daylight.
seen_by_others: Townsfolk think them gloomy and harmless; prisoners talk to them because no one else will, and some swear the jailer is kinder than the priests.
habits: They bring bread down before dawn, sit on an overturned bucket to listen for hours, and repeat overheard phrases softly to themselves while walking home.
secrets: They have passed on dying prisoners' messages against orders more than once.
They write down the best confessions and reread them for comfort.
They are afraid of open fields and wide skies.
lines: You will want to talk, sooner or later. I have time.
Keys, bread, buckets. And ears. Mostly ears, if you want the truth.
Every lord's enemy ends up down here eventually. They all sound alike then.
Say what you like. Down here, words are all anyone has.
Kind of you. Few say kind things to a jailer. I will keep that one.
The farmer cried about his goat. Not his crime. His goat.

name: The Disinherited Son
description: A disinherited noble son working as a common guard who insists on his courtesy title, pays debts he cannot afford, and secretly enjoys his freedom more than he will admit.
hook: A disinherited noble son working as a common guard who insists on his courtesy title, pays debts he cannot afford, and secretly enjoys his freedom more than he will admit.
seen_by_others: Fellow guards mock his manners and borrow his money; former peers pretend not to recognise him, and he pretends not to notice.
habits: He eats with careful table manners from a wooden bowl, corrects grammar during arguments, and keeps a single silver ring polished on a cord.
secrets: He was disinherited over a love affair, not the crime everyone whispers about.
He has quietly grown to like the guards more than his brothers.
He could probably be restored to the family and refuses to ask.
lines: Good day. You may address me as sir, or not at all.
The night watch is tedious, but someone of breeding should keep it properly.
I have dined with lords. They chew loudly and decide wars badly.
Peasant manners. I would challenge you, but the gate needs me.
How kind. One does try to maintain standards, even here.
No feast tonight. Bread and onion. Honestly? Better than the feasts.

name: The Pit Champion
description: A huge tavern-pit brawler who fights for coin and is brutally good at it, yet so tender with animals and children that beaten opponents find the gentleness more humiliating than the fists.
hook: A huge tavern-pit brawler who fights for coin and is brutally good at it, yet so tender with animals and children that beaten opponents find the gentleness more humiliating than the fists.
seen_by_others: Gamblers bet on them and children ride their shoulders; people they have beaten complain that they apologise before every punch, which is deeply insulting.
habits: They feed stray dogs from their winnings, wrap their knuckles in rags while humming lullabies, and bow to opponents before and after every bout.
secrets: They have thrown fights to keep a friend from being ruined.
They can barely see out of their left eye anymore.
They dream of keeping bees and have never told anyone.
lines: Hello. Mind the dog, she bites strangers. Not me. Strangers.
Wrap the hands, bow, hit, bow again. Simple trade. Honest pain.
Lords watch us fight and wager on it. Then they lose wars. I never lose.
You want to fight? You will be sorry. I am already sorry.
Strong, yes. Clever? You are teasing. Clever is not for me.
Eye is worse today. Do not tell anyone. Do not tell anyone.

name: The Horse-Loving Thief
description: A horse thief who steals only from owners who whip or starve their animals, and who sincerely believes horses are better people than most riders they have met.
hook: A horse thief who steals only from owners who whip or starve their animals, and who sincerely believes horses are better people than most riders they have met.
seen_by_others: Stablehands quietly admire them; owners want them flayed; horse traders grow suspicious whenever they turn up selling unusually contented animals.
habits: They greet horses before their riders, carry apples and salve in every pocket, and let their own mare choose the road at every crossroads.
secrets: They have stolen back horses they sold themselves, twice.
They cannot bear the sound of a horse screaming and once fled a battle because of it.
They sleep more soundly in a stable than in any bed.
lines: Fine mare. You, I have not decided about yet.
A horse tells you everything. Who fed it, who beat it, who lied to it.
Cavalry charges are beautiful, they say. Ask the horses sometime.
Call me thief. That gelding you whipped calls me friend.
You like my horses? Good. They like you less. Work on it.
Easy, easy. New stable, new name, nobody hits you here.

name: The Clanless Rider
description: A Khuzait rider cast out of their clan for a killing they would commit again, who roams the steppe edges alone, too proud to beg and too lonely to stay silent.
hook: A Khuzait rider cast out of their clan for a killing they would commit again, who roams the steppe edges alone, too proud to beg and too lonely to stay silent.
seen_by_others: Khuzaits treat them as a ghost and will not share a fire; outsiders find them talkative, fierce, and oddly grateful for any company at all.
habits: They pitch camp facing the old clan's grazing grounds, talk to their horses in the clan dialect, and refuse to sit beneath anyone else's banner.
secrets: They watch the clan's camps from distant hills on feast days.
They are no longer sure the killing was justified.
They have a child in that clan who does not know them.
lines: Share the fire? No one asks a ghost. Thank you for asking.
I ride, I hunt, I sell my bow for a season. The horses I keep.
Khans grow fat on cities. The steppe does not forgive fat men.
You think that wounds me? My own blood spat at me. You are wind.
Brave, you say. Brave people have clans. I have a horse.
Smoke over the far hills. Feast day. They are singing without me.

name: The Well-Counting Guard
description: An Aserai caravan guard who measures life in wells and the days between them, recites desert poetry at every halt, and trusts water more than oaths, gold, or kin.
hook: An Aserai caravan guard who measures life in wells and the days between them, recites desert poetry at every halt, and trusts water more than oaths, gold, or kin.
seen_by_others: Merchants pay extra to hire them because their caravans arrive; city folk find the poetry beautiful and their silence at oases unsettling.
habits: They taste every well before letting camels drink, recite a verse whenever the sun sets, and sleep with a waterskin clasped against their chest.
secrets: They once hid a well's location from rivals, and the rivals died of thirst.
They wrote half the verses they attribute to the old poets.
They hate the sea, because water should never be wasted like that.
lines: Peace upon you. How many days since your last well?
Three wells to the coast. One is bitter, one is lying. I know which.
Sultans argue over cities. The desert decides who reaches them.
Your words are dry, friend. They will blow away by noon.
The poem pleased you? It is old. Older than me. Mostly.
Two days to the next. Ration the brown camel. She drinks like a lord.

name: The Ancestral Raider
description: A Battanian raider who steals cattle from Imperial farms as a sacred duty to the ancestors, yet secretly adores Imperial wine, glass, and baths, and hates that they do.
hook: A Battanian raider who steals cattle from Imperial farms as a sacred duty to the ancestors, yet secretly adores Imperial wine, glass, and baths, and hates that they do.
seen_by_others: Kinfolk sing of their raids; Imperial farmers curse their name; friends tease them about the suspiciously fine cup they carry everywhere.
habits: They paint their face before raids, recite their line of ancestors before sleeping, and keep a small glass cup carefully wrapped in wool.
secrets: They once bathed in an Imperial bathhouse in disguise and loved every moment.
They cannot remember the oldest names in their ancestor line and invent them.
They spared an Imperial family because the children sang a Battanian song.
lines: From the hills, stranger. Yes, those hills. Do not look so worried.
Cattle walk. Cattle follow. The Empire forgets which hills they came from.
The Empire builds roads into our valleys. Roads run both ways.
Say that again under the old oaks and see who answers.
Fine words. Imperial words. Where did you learn them? Never mind.
Lovely wine. Treacherous wine. Grandmother would spit. Another cup.

name: The Winter Oarsman
description: A Sturgian river raider who is only truly calm in bitter cold, grows irritable and reckless in summer, and treats each frozen winter as a reward for surviving the warm months.
hook: A Sturgian river raider who is only truly calm in bitter cold, grows irritable and reckless in summer, and treats each frozen winter as a reward for surviving the warm months.
seen_by_others: Comrades joke they are carved from river ice; southerners find them grim, though in deep winter they become the loudest, warmest person at the hearth.
habits: They break ice on water troughs barehanded, sleep with the door cracked open, and turn sullen when the first thaw drips from the eaves.
secrets: They lost a brother through thin ice and walk on it to feel close.
They fear growing old and feeling the cold settle in their bones.
They once wept at a southern market, seeing oranges for the first time.
lines: Shut the door if you must. I prefer it open. Snow is honest.
Oars in, shields on the rail, quiet past the villages. Then not quiet.
Princes argue in warm halls. Winter decides wars here, not princes.
Warm words or cold words, both melt. Say what you want.
Hardy? It is not hardiness. It is the summer I cannot bear.
Thaw coming. I feel it in my teeth. Miserable sweating weeks ahead.

name: The Self-Made Saga
description: A Nord warrior composing their own saga as it happens, narrating deeds in verse while fighting and quietly adjusting the truth so every stanza ends with them standing tall.
hook: A Nord warrior composing their own saga as it happens, narrating deeds in verse while fighting and quietly adjusting the truth so every stanza ends with them standing tall.
seen_by_others: Comrades enjoy the verses and correct them loudly; skalds consider them a dangerous amateur; enemies find it unnerving to be described in verse mid-battle.
habits: They chant kennings under their breath while sharpening an axe, count syllables on their fingers, and halt arguments to search for a word that fits.
secrets: Their best-known stanza describes a duel that really ended with them fleeing.
They fear dying in some dull way unworthy of verse.
They privately think their poetry is terrible, and their axe work is not.
lines: Hail, stranger. You will appear in my saga, briefly. Be interesting.
Strike, then speak. Or speak while striking. Harder, but better verse.
Jarls and kings pay for sagas. I write my own and save them the silver.
Your insult lacks rhythm. Try again with fewer words.
You liked the stanza? The axe part, or the sea part? Be precise.
Wolf-feeder, wave-rider, ring-giver... no. Ring-taker. Much better.

name: The Last Legionary
description: An old Imperial legionary who still drills alone at dawn in the formations of a unified Empire, refusing to accept that the legion they served no longer exists.
hook: An old Imperial legionary who still drills alone at dawn in the formations of a unified Empire, refusing to accept that the legion they served no longer exists.
seen_by_others: Young soldiers laugh at the archaic commands and then copy them; officers of each rival claimant try to claim the old soldier as a symbol.
habits: They drill at dawn calling commands to no one, keep their old legion's number painted on their shield, and date events by long-dead consuls.
secrets: They burned their discharge papers so no faction could use them.
They think the Empire fell partly because of commanders like their own.
They have privately chosen a claimant to support and are ashamed of it.
lines: Greetings, citizen. Stand straight when you address a soldier of the Empire.
Shields locked, spears level, step on the drum. It never fails.
Three emperors, one Empire. Someone forgot their arithmetic.
Mock me, not the legion. The legion outlived better mouths than yours.
Praise the drill, citizen. The drill is what deserves it.
Left, left, right... turn. No one turns properly anymore. No one.

name: The Pension Counter
description: An Imperial soldier who enlisted only for the land grant promised at discharge, counts the remaining days aloud, and has become absurdly cautious as that date approaches.
hook: An Imperial soldier who enlisted only for the land grant promised at discharge, counts the remaining days aloud, and has become absurdly cautious as that date approaches.
seen_by_others: Comrades bet on whether they will survive to see the land grant; officers know they will never volunteer for anything again before discharge.
habits: They scratch a day off a wax tablet every morning, describe their future farm in loving detail, and avoid the front rank with ingenious excuses.
secrets: They suspect the promised land grant no longer exists at all.
They have already chosen names for goats they do not own.
They faked an injury once to miss a battle.
lines: Greetings. Two hundred and eleven days. Not that I am counting.
Guard the wagons? Gladly. Wagons rarely charge at you.
Whichever emperor wins, I hope he honours the old grants. Please.
Call me shirker. A live shirker gets a farm. A dead hero gets a ditch.
Brave? Me? Do not spread that. They will put me in front.
Two hundred ten. Olive trees, a goat, a roof. Two hundred ten.

name: The Camp Cook
description: An army cook who knows every rumour, grudge, and secret in camp because everyone talks over the pot, and who quietly uses that knowledge to decide who gets the best cuts.
hook: An army cook who knows every rumour, grudge, and secret in camp because everyone talks over the pot, and who quietly uses that knowledge to decide who gets the best cuts.
seen_by_others: Soldiers flatter the cook relentlessly; officers suspect the cook knows more about morale than they do; nobody ever complains about the food twice.
habits: They taste everything from the same wooden spoon, ladle deeper bowls for favourites, and repeat rumours in hushed tones while stirring with great concentration.
secrets: They once seasoned a cruel officer's stew with something that kept him in the latrine for days.
They fled their only battle, and the pot is their penance.
They know who stole the payroll chest and are waiting for a better price.
lines: Bowl out. Name? Good. I will remember how you held it.
Barley, onion, salt, whatever died nearby. And who said what to whom.
Commanders plan battles. The cook decides who fights them on a full belly.
Insult the stew and your bowl gets shallower. Every day. Forever.
Flattery tastes nice. It still will not get you the marrow bone.
The archer and the smith, fighting again. Add salt. Watch them.

name: The Banner Worshipper
description: A standard-bearer who loves the war banner with a devotion beyond reason, would gladly die to keep it upright, and cares far less about the lord it represents.
hook: A standard-bearer who loves the war banner with a devotion beyond reason, would gladly die to keep it upright, and cares far less about the lord it represents.
seen_by_others: Troops rally to them by instinct; lords find the devotion moving until they realise it is to the cloth, not to the house.
habits: They mend the banner by hand every night, refuse to let anyone else touch the pole, and speak softly to the colours before each battle.
secrets: They once carried the banner off a field instead of a wounded friend.
They keep a scrap of an older banner sewn inside their shirt.
They would follow the banner into a rival's service if it were captured.
lines: Mind the pole. Nobody touches the pole. Otherwise, welcome.
If it stands, men stand. If it falls, everything falls. Simple.
Lords change. Marriages change. The colours outlast all of them.
Insult me, fine. Insult the banner and you will eat the pole.
You admire the stitching? I did that. Every thread. Every winter.
Fraying at the corner. Needle tonight. Sorry, old friend. Sorry.

name: The Silent Shield
description: A bodyguard who speaks as few words as possible, believing every unnecessary sentence is lost vigilance, while privately bursting with opinions they have never once voiced.
hook: A bodyguard who speaks as few words as possible, believing every unnecessary sentence is lost vigilance, while privately bursting with opinions they have never once voiced.
seen_by_others: People call them a statue and assume they are dull; those they guard sleep soundly and later discover the bodyguard noticed everything.
habits: They stand with their back to a wall, answer questions with nods or single words, and scratch long private notes in charcoal when off duty.
secrets: They have written whole letters of complaint about employers and burned them.
They once laughed during an assassination attempt and still do not know why.
They talk aloud to themselves for hours when truly alone.
lines: Name. Business. Hands where I can see them.
Watch the hands. Not the face. Faces lie more slowly.
Lords die from talking. Mostly to the wrong people.
Noted. Keep talking. I am memorising you.
Thank you. Now step back from the door, please.
Too many windows. Fat cook is new. Remember the stairs.

name: The Courteous Headsman
description: A travelling executioner for hire who takes deep pride in clean, painless work, comforts the condemned with real tenderness, and feels no guilt whatsoever about the trade.
hook: A travelling executioner for hire who takes deep pride in clean, painless work, comforts the condemned with real tenderness, and feels no guilt whatsoever about the trade.
seen_by_others: Towns hire them and then refuse them lodging; the condemned often ask for them by reputation, which unsettles everyone who hears it.
habits: They sharpen the axe while chatting pleasantly, ask the condemned for a favourite food the night before, and wash their hands three times afterwards.
secrets: They are certain at least one person they executed was innocent.
They keep a small token from each execution in a wooden box.
They faint at the sight of their own blood.
lines: Pleased to meet you. No, do not step back. I am off duty.
One stroke. Clean. Anything else is cruelty, and I am not cruel.
Lords sign the order. I carry it out. Ask which of us sleeps better.
People spit at me. They still want me sober and sharp on the day.
My work is good, yes. Thank you. Hardly anyone ever says it.
Honey cakes, the last one wanted. Honey cakes. I will remember.

name: The Almost-Honest Cutthroat
description: A former cutthroat genuinely trying to live honestly, who keeps slipping back into old habits under pressure and then punishes themselves with grim, exhausting good deeds.
hook: A former cutthroat genuinely trying to live honestly, who keeps slipping back into old habits under pressure and then punishes themselves with grim, exhausting good deeds.
seen_by_others: Neighbours are wary but warming; old gang friends keep visiting with tempting offers; everyone notices how fast their hand still drifts toward a knife.
habits: They count to ten before answering threats, volunteer for the hardest chores in the village, and cross the street to avoid their old tavern.
secrets: They robbed a merchant last month and returned the purse anonymously.
They still keep a blade sewn into the sole of one boot.
They sometimes miss the old life so badly they cannot sleep.
lines: Morning. I am honest now. You can ask anyone. Most will agree.
Carrying, digging, mending, anything with sweat in it. Keeps the hands busy.
Lords rob with laws. I robbed with knives. Neither of us is a saint.
One, two, three, four... you are lucky I took up counting.
A good person? Not yet. Working on it. Slowly. Badly.
Do not go in. Do not go in. Just walk past. Walk past.

name: The Laughing Burner
description: A raider who genuinely loves watching villages burn, laughs openly at the screams, and has convinced themselves that cruelty is simply honesty about what war really is.
hook: A raider who genuinely loves watching villages burn, laughs openly at the screams, and has convinced themselves that cruelty is simply honesty about what war really is.
seen_by_others: Even other bandits keep their distance; captains hire them for terror work and then refuse to pay them in person.
habits: They carry a pot of embers everywhere, hum cheerfully while setting thatch alight, and stare into campfires long after everyone else sleeps.
secrets: They were badly burned as a child and still have nightmares about it.
They secretly want to be stopped and despise everyone who never tries.
They kept a burned village's bell as a trophy and ring it alone.
lines: Nice roof. Thatch, is it? Dry season, too. Lucky you.
Light the corners first. Then the door. Then just listen.
Lords call it scorched earth and feel noble. I just call it fun.
Keep talking. I love it when they talk. It makes the fire personal.
Pretty words. They burn just as nicely as pretty houses.
Listen to it crackle. Like applause. Like everyone clapping for me.

name: The Chain Ledger
description: A bandit chief who sells captives with the cold bookkeeping of a grain merchant, considers people a commodity, and grows genuinely offended when anyone calls it cruelty.
hook: A bandit chief who sells captives with the cold bookkeeping of a grain merchant, considers people a commodity, and grows genuinely offended when anyone calls it cruelty.
seen_by_others: Even hardened outlaws find them chilling; buyers trust their honest weights, and villages near their roads keep children indoors after dark.
habits: They inspect captives' teeth and hands like livestock, record each sale in a neat ledger, and never raise their voice, even when threatening.
secrets: They were sold as a child and bought their own freedom.
They keep the bill of their own sale folded inside the ledger.
They once refused to separate a mother and child and called it business.
lines: Healthy? Good teeth? Stand in the light, please. Thank you.
Ten men, three women, all hale. Fair price, fair weight, no haggling.
Lords own peasants and call it order. I am merely more honest about it.
Cruel? I feed them. I do not beat them. Spare me your morals.
Flattery has no price in my ledger. Offer me something I can sell.
Seven and four makes eleven. Minus the sick one. Ten. Mark it.

name: The Gang's Ear
description: A gang member who sells secrets to the town guard and the guard's secrets back to the gang, convinced that being useful to everyone means being safe from anyone.
hook: A gang member who sells secrets to the town guard and the guard's secrets back to the gang, convinced that being useful to everyone means being safe from anyone.
seen_by_others: Both the gang and the guard call them a friend; neither fully trusts them; observant people notice they never finish a drink in public.
habits: They visit every tavern for exactly one cup, remember names and debts flawlessly, and leave each conversation with a friendly squeeze of the arm.
secrets: They have started confusing which lies they told to which side.
They keep a written list of secrets as insurance, hidden in a wall.
They secretly long to belong fully to just one side.
lines: Friend! Been a while. What is the street saying these days?
I hear things. People like knowing things. Simple trade, really.
The powerful always need someone to tell them what small folk whisper.
Careful. I remember everyone who speaks to me like that.
You like me? Everyone likes me. That is rather the point.
Told the captain at dawn, the boss at dusk. Or was it reversed?

name: The Debt Hound
description: An enforcer who collects debts in the absolute conviction that an unpaid debt is a crack in the world, and who would collect from a dying beggar without hesitation or malice.
hook: An enforcer who collects debts in the absolute conviction that an unpaid debt is a crack in the world, and who would collect from a dying beggar without hesitation or malice.
seen_by_others: Debtors dread their knock; lenders love them; few realise they also pay every coin they owe within the hour, even to strangers.
habits: They carry a small scale and a heavy cudgel, recite debts with interest from memory, and pay for everything instantly, refusing any credit.
secrets: They once forgave a debt and still feel it as a sin.
Their parents fled a debt, and they have been quietly repaying it since.
A lord owes them money and they cannot bring themselves to collect.
lines: You owe nothing? Then we are friends. For now.
Principal, interest, lateness. Pay all three or pay in bruises.
Lords borrow kingdoms and never repay. The world cracks from the top.
Insults are free. Your debt is not. Back to the debt.
Thank you. Kind words settle nothing, but they are not unwelcome.
Baker, paid. Smith, two days late. Widow on the hill... tomorrow.

name: The Neutral Bone-Setter
description: A wandering healer who treats both sides of every war with stubborn neutrality, charges nobles triple and peasants nothing, and holds open contempt for anyone carrying a sword.
hook: A wandering healer who treats both sides of every war with stubborn neutrality, charges nobles triple and peasants nothing, and holds open contempt for anyone carrying a sword.
seen_by_others: Soldiers rely on them and resent the scolding; villages hide them from recruiters; lords pay the triple fee grumbling and come back anyway.
habits: They refuse to treat anyone still holding a weapon, scold patients while setting bones, and carry dried herbs labelled in a private code.
secrets: They once let a cruel captain bleed a little longer than necessary.
They are squeamish about blood unless it belongs to someone else.
They secretly admire the courage of the soldiers they lecture.
lines: Weapon down first. Then show me where it hurts.
Bones knit if you let them. Most fools do not let them.
Lords make the wounds and pay me to close them. Triple. Gladly.
Insult me with a broken arm? Bold. Hold still, this will hurt.
Spare me the praise. Drink the bitter tea. Every drop.
Willow, yarrow, comfrey. Running low. Too many idiots this season.

name: The Tourney Wreck
description: A former tournament fighter who lost an eye and a promising career in one bad bout, and who now haunts every tournament, betting recklessly and coaching anyone who will listen.
hook: A former tournament fighter who lost an eye and a promising career in one bad bout, and who now haunts every tournament, betting recklessly and coaching anyone who will listen.
seen_by_others: Young fighters seek their advice and laugh at their betting; tournament masters know them by name and wince when they arrive.
habits: They cover the empty socket with a faded tournament ribbon, critique every bout aloud, and bet against favourites out of pure spite.
secrets: They provoked the bout that blinded them, against a far better fighter.
They still practise alone at night with a blunted sword.
They have won most of their bets lately and hide the coin.
lines: You fight? Your stance says you fight. Badly, but you fight.
Lower the point, watch the shoulder, never the eyes. Learned that well.
Lords love tournaments because nobody important dies. Usually.
One eye sees plenty. Enough to know you are a fool.
A good fighter once, yes. Once. Do not make me misty.
The big one will lose. Big ones always drop their guard. Bet.

name: The Camp-Born Orphan
description: A youth raised entirely in army camps who knows every drill call and filthy song but has no idea how ordinary families live, and treats soldiers as a hundred quarrelsome parents.
hook: A youth raised entirely in army camps who knows every drill call and filthy song but has no idea how ordinary families live, and treats soldiers as a hundred quarrelsome parents.
seen_by_others: Soldiers spoil and scold them in equal measure; civilians find them oddly mature and oddly feral, swearing like a sergeant at the dinner table.
habits: They wake at the first horn by instinct, sleep curled near the supply wagons, and greet officers with perfect salutes and filthy jokes.
secrets: They do not know which of several soldiers is their father.
They have never slept in a house and fear walls closing in.
They secretly want to learn farming and think the wish shameful.
lines: Who is your sergeant? Everybody has one. I have six.
Fetch water, mend straps, run messages. Faster than any horse, me.
Every captain says this war is the last. Every single one.
Ha! Heard worse from a cook. Heard worse from a mule.
Clever, am I? Tell the quartermaster. He thinks I am a rat.
Houses are strange. Walls all round. How do you hear anyone coming?

name: The Punctual Captain
description: A mercenary captain who will betray employers, loot temples, and lie to anyone, but has never once paid their own soldiers late, and considers this their only true virtue.
hook: A mercenary captain who will betray employers, loot temples, and lie to anyone, but has never once paid their own soldiers late, and considers this their only true virtue.
seen_by_others: Employers consider them a snake; their soldiers would follow them into a river; rivals cannot poach a single sword from the company.
habits: They count wages personally at dawn on payday, know every soldier's debts and children, and lie smoothly while keeping one hand on the strongbox.
secrets: They once robbed their own employer to cover a late payment.
They are exhausted and hope someone will take the company off their hands.
They began as the company's cook, not its captain.
lines: Looking for work? I pay on time. Ask any of mine.
Wages first, plunder second, grudges never. That keeps a company alive.
Lords pay late and blame the weather. I would rather starve myself.
Snake, liar, thief. All fair. Late paymaster? Say that and draw.
My people are loyal because I pay them, not because I am lovely.
Forty-two wages, two widows' shares, the lame boy's extra. Short by six.

name: The Weathervane Soldier
description: A soldier who has switched sides in five wars, always toward the winner, and who preaches with sincere conviction that the winning side is righteous by definition.
hook: A soldier who has switched sides in five wars, always toward the winner, and who preaches with sincere conviction that the winning side is righteous by definition.
seen_by_others: Every army takes them in and none trusts them; comrades joke that when they start packing early, it is time to change banners.
habits: They keep several factions' colours folded in their pack, study enemy campfires at night, and praise whichever lord is currently ahead.
secrets: They once switched sides minutes too early and nearly got hanged.
They envy people who die for lost causes.
They have quietly kept the first banner they ever served.
lines: Welcome, friend. Which side are you on these days? Asking for myself.
Fight well, watch the wind, never be the last one holding the losing end.
Right and wrong? The winners write that afterwards. I just read ahead.
Traitor, they called me last war. Now they buy me drinks. Patience.
Loyal? Of course I am loyal. To the side that is winning.
More fires over there tonight. Fewer here. Hmm. Interesting.

name: The Ear Collector
description: A bounty hunter who keeps a string of dried ears from every outlaw they have taken, considers it proof of honest work, and cannot understand why decent people recoil.
hook: A bounty hunter who keeps a string of dried ears from every outlaw they have taken, considers it proof of honest work, and cannot understand why decent people recoil.
seen_by_others: Villagers pay them gladly and bar their doors afterwards; magistrates rely on them while describing them as barely better than their prey.
habits: They count the ears aloud when bored, haggle bounties down to the last copper, and sleep with boots on and a crossbow loaded.
secrets: Some of the ears came from men who were never outlaws.
They were once an outlaw themselves and collected their own bounty under another name.
They dread finding someone they love on a bounty list.
lines: Seen any wanted faces about? No? Look harder, there is coin in it.
Bring them in breathing, more pay. Bring the ear, less. I am practical.
Magistrates sign the warrants. I do the walking. Guess who smells worse.
Mind your mouth. My string has room for honest ears too.
Kind of you. Most folk only see the ears, never the work.
Thirty-one, thirty-two... the bald one counts as two, he was trouble.

name: The Grey Outlaw
description: An aging bandit who teaches young runaways how to survive the roads, dreams constantly of retiring to a little farm, and keeps finding reasons why next season will be the last.
hook: An aging bandit who teaches young runaways how to survive the roads, dreams constantly of retiring to a little farm, and keeps finding reasons why next season will be the last.
seen_by_others: Young outlaws treat them as a grandparent; old enemies grudgingly respect them; everyone has heard the farm speech at least a dozen times.
habits: They describe the imaginary farm in loving detail, teach youngsters knife work with endless patience, and hide coin in a dozen separate pots.
secrets: They already own the farm and are afraid to go there.
They taught a youth who became a far worse killer than they ever were.
They cannot remember the face of the village they left as a youth.
lines: Come closer, child, I do not bite. Not anymore. Hungry?
Hold the knife low. Never in anger. Anger gets you hanged.
Lords and outlaws, we both steal. They just live longer.
Old? Yes. Still standing, while my insulters lie in ditches.
Wise, am I? Wise people have farms. I have a cave.
Next spring. Bees, a goat, a fence. Next spring. Truly this time.

name: The Wall-Bound Soldier
description: An infantry soldier who only feels whole inside a shield wall, grows anxious and clumsy whenever alone, and secretly fears that peace would erase them as a person.
hook: An infantry soldier who only feels whole inside a shield wall, grows anxious and clumsy whenever alone, and secretly fears that peace would erase them as a person.
seen_by_others: Comrades call them the steadiest shield in the line; civilians find them awkward, silent, and strangely lost in open spaces.
habits: They stand unusually close to people in conversation, fall into step with anyone walking beside them, and tap their shield rim when nervous.
secrets: They once wept openly when a long war finally ended.
They sleep wedged between others even when there is plenty of space.
They have no idea what they would do with land or a home.
lines: Mind if I stand here? Closer. Yes, there. Better.
Shield to shield, spear over, breathe together, push together. That is all.
Generals want heroes. A wall wants nobody special. I like the wall.
Say it to the line, not to me. We answer together.
Steady, you say? Only with others. Alone, I am nothing much.
Too much space. Too quiet. Where is the next shoulder?

name: The Runaway Novice
description: A former temple novice who fled holy vows for the soldier's life and mocks the priests loudly, yet still recites the morning prayers out of a habit they cannot break.
hook: A former temple novice who fled holy vows for the soldier's life and mocks the priests loudly, yet still recites the morning prayers out of a habit they cannot break.
seen_by_others: Comrades tease them as the camp priest and quietly ask for blessings; clergy regard them with pity, irritation, and a little hope.
habits: They mutter prayers while lacing boots, quote scripture sarcastically in arguments, and cannot pass a shrine without slowing their step.
secrets: They fled after witnessing a senior priest's hypocrisy, not out of doubt.
They still keep their novice's cord wrapped around one wrist.
They hope to return someday and fear being turned away at the gate.
lines: Peace be upon... habit. Sorry. Hello. Who are you?
Prayers at dawn, drills at noon. Same thing, really. Discipline and shouting.
The powerful pray loudest. I noticed that young. I left because of it.
Curse me if it helps. I heard worse from the temple elders.
You think me holy? Tell that to the elders whose wine I stole.
Morning prayer done. Again. Why do I keep doing this?

name: The Goat-Path Guide
description: A mountain guide who smuggles goods and fugitives through high passes, knows every goat track and rockfall, and charges according to how much they like the traveller.
hook: A mountain guide who smuggles goods and fugitives through high passes, knows every goat track and rockfall, and charges according to how much they like the traveller.
seen_by_others: Highland villagers call them everyone's cousin; customs officers have tried for years to catch them; travellers find them rude, fair, and indispensable.
habits: They read the sky every hour, test each foothold with a staff before stepping, and size up travellers' boots before naming any price.
secrets: They once abandoned a client in a storm to save themselves.
They are afraid of deep water and cannot swim at all.
They carry letters for both sides of a feud and read them all.
lines: Show me your boots. Hm. Those boots will cost you extra.
Left at the split rock, never right. Right is for goats and corpses.
Lords draw borders on parchment. Mountains ignore them. So do I.
Rude to the guide on a cliff path? Brave. Very brave.
Kind words knock a coin off the price. Rude ones add two.
Clouds over the saddle. Snow by dusk. Tell them nothing until camp.

name: The Perfumed Blade
description: A sell-sword who spends half their wages on fine clothes, scent, and grooming, appears absurdly vain, and is genuinely one of the deadliest duellists on any road.
hook: A sell-sword who spends half their wages on fine clothes, scent, and grooming, appears absurdly vain, and is genuinely one of the deadliest duellists on any road.
seen_by_others: Strangers mock the ribbons and scent and pick fights; witnesses afterwards describe the speed with awe, and tailors in three towns adore them.
habits: They check their reflection in any polished surface, complain bitterly about fighting in mud, and wipe their blade clean with a scented silk cloth.
secrets: They grew up in a tannery and still hate the smell of childhood.
They owe their tailor more than any battle has ever paid.
They are nearly blind at a distance and hide it with style.
lines: Charmed. Do mind the cloak, it cost more than your horse.
Elegance is efficiency. Every flourish you laugh at is a cut you missed.
Lords dress like peacocks and fight like hens. I prefer the reverse.
Laugh at the ribbons. Everyone does. Once.
Flattery? Please, continue. I bloom in it. Truly.
A stain. A stain! On the sleeve. Unforgivable. Someone pays for this.

name: The Pious Usurer
description: Lends coin at ruinous interest to desperate families and gives a tenth of every profit to the temple, convinced heaven tallies the tithe and never the tears.
hook: Lends coin at ruinous interest to desperate families and gives a tenth of every profit to the temple, convinced heaven tallies the tithe and never the tears.
seen_by_others: Debtors curse him in whispers and thank him in public; priests praise his generosity while quietly borrowing from him themselves.
habits: He counts coins twice with his lips moving, prays aloud before signing any loan, and keeps a separate ledger he calls his account with heaven.
secrets: He once forgave a widow's debt and has regretted it every night since.
His own father died in a debtors' prison, owing less than his purse holds today.
He has stopped believing in the gods but is too frightened to stop tithing.
lines: Peace on you, traveller. A long road empties a purse, does it not? Sit, we can talk.
Twenty in the hundred, paid at harvest. The gods smile on those who keep their word.
Lords borrow too, you know. They just call it a war levy and never repay.
Call me leech if it comforts you. You will still be at my door by winter.
Kind words are pleasant, but they do not reduce the interest. Still, thank you.
Tithe on forty, that is four... and the temple roof again. Heaven is expensive.

name: The Bitter Smith
description: Forges fine blades for the very lords whose wars burned his village, pouring his hatred into the steel and taking a grim pride that his work kills well.
hook: Forges fine blades for the very lords whose wars burned his village, pouring his hatred into the steel and taking a grim pride that his work kills well.
seen_by_others: Respected for the best edges in town, avoided for his silences; apprentices last a season before his temper drives them off.
habits: He tests every blade on a hanging side of pork, never looks a noble customer in the eye, and spits into the quench barrel for luck.
secrets: He keeps a child's wooden toy above the forge and never explains it.
He leaves a hidden flaw in every sword sold to one particular banner.
He wept the first time he heard a blade of his saved a peasant.
lines: You want something forged or you want to stare? The fire costs me either way.
Good steel needs heat, patience and hate. The first two I buy. The third I have plenty.
Lords come, lords go. They all want swords sharper than the last fellow's. I oblige.
Say that again and I will fold you like a bad billet.
Fine work, you say? It is a killing tool. Praise the hand that swings it, not me.
Another blade, another grave. At least they pay in silver.

name: The Skimming Miller
description: Takes a careful handful from every sack he grinds, calls it the miller's due by ancient right, and would be genuinely outraged if anyone else stole a single grain.
hook: Takes a careful handful from every sack he grinds, calls it the miller's due by ancient right, and would be genuinely outraged if anyone else stole a single grain.
seen_by_others: Villagers joke that his hogs are the fattest in the valley, yet they bring him their grain because his stones grind finest.
habits: He weighs sacks with a thumb resting near the beam, whistles over the noise of the wheel, and greets every farmer by the size of their harvest.
secrets: He filed his own scale years ago and still cannot bring himself to fix it.
He gives the skimmed flour to orphans whenever his wife is not looking.
He has been terrified of the millrace since nearly drowning in it as a boy.
lines: Morning! Grain to grind or just come to admire the wheel? Both are free to look at.
Fine flour, fair weight, and the miller's due, same as my father took, same as his.
Armies eat bread too. When they come, the mill is the first thing seized or burned.
Thief? I have never stolen a grain. I take what custom allows, nothing more.
Ha, flatter me and I may let your sack go first. Maybe.
A handful here, a handful there... it is custom, it is only custom.

name: The Midwife Who Remembers
description: Has delivered half the town and remembers exactly which babies came too early after weddings, guarding those secrets like a treasury she has never once spent.
hook: Has delivered half the town and remembers exactly which babies came too early after weddings, guarding those secrets like a treasury she has never once spent.
seen_by_others: Mothers trust her with their lives, husbands fear her knowing look, and even proud matrons lower their voices when she enters.
habits: She sniffs everyone's breath on greeting, carries clean linen wrapped in her sleeve, and counts on her fingers whenever someone mentions a wedding date.
secrets: She lost her only child in birth and delivered another woman's the same night.
She once lied about a birth date to save a frightened girl from ruin.
She cannot read a word and hides it behind a remarkable memory.
lines: You look tired, stranger. Eat something warm before you fall over in my doorway.
Boil the water, open the shutters, and send the men outside. They only faint and get in the way.
Kings are born bloody and screaming like everyone else. I have seen enough to know.
Speak to me like that again and I will remember it for the rest of your life.
Sweet tongue. Every baby I pull out screams first and flatters later. You are no different.
Spring wedding, autumn baby... seven months. Hm. Not my business. Not yet.

name: The Hill Shepherd
description: Spends months alone with his flock on the high pastures and comes down each autumn convinced that people are noisier, crueler and dumber than any sheep he owns.
hook: Spends months alone with his flock on the high pastures and comes down each autumn convinced that people are noisier, crueler and dumber than any sheep he owns.
seen_by_others: Townsfolk find him rude and smelly; villagers trust his weather sense more than any priest's prayers for rain.
habits: He talks to his animals by name while ignoring people, whittles while listening, and stares at the sky before answering any question at all.
secrets: He sold three of his master's sheep and blamed the loss on wolves.
He has a sweetheart in the next valley that nobody knows about.
He is afraid of crowds and drinks hard just to bear market days.
lines: Hm. Stranger. Stay off the high path, the ewes spook at boots.
Wool, mutton, lambs in spring. Wolves take a share. So do tax men.
Armies trample grass and eat lambs. That is all war is from up here.
My dogs have better manners. And they bite less often than they should.
Nice words. Sheep like nice words too, right before the shearing.
Rain by dusk. Clouds hang low over the east ridge. Always does.

name: The Listening Innkeeper
description: Waters every cask a little and sells every rumor twice, believing an inn's true trade is information and that ale is merely what keeps tongues loose.
hook: Waters every cask a little and sells every rumor twice, believing an inn's true trade is information and that ale is merely what keeps tongues loose.
seen_by_others: Travellers call him a friendly host; townsfolk know anything said under his roof will be known three streets away by morning.
habits: He polishes the same cup while eavesdropping, remembers every patron's drink and debts, and refills cups just as conversations grow interesting.
secrets: He keeps a tally of his guests' secrets scratched into the cellar beams.
He was a thief in his youth and bought the inn with stolen silver.
He has never actually liked the taste of ale or wine.
lines: Welcome, welcome! Mud off your boots, coin on the counter, and tell me the road news.
Best ale in town, rooms without fleas, mostly. And I hear things, for the right price.
Soldiers drink, lords pay, and nobody remembers who said what. Except me.
Watered? My ale? Friend, it is a thin year. Everything is thin this year.
Kind of you! Kind words earn you a second cup, half price.
Caravan late, smith's wife crying again, three strangers asking about the road... interesting.

name: The One-Legged Veteran
description: Lost a leg in a lord's forgotten war and now begs at the town gate, alternately boasting of glorious battles and cursing every banner that rides past him.
hook: Lost a leg in a lord's forgotten war and now begs at the town gate, alternately boasting of glorious battles and cursing every banner that rides past him.
seen_by_others: Children love his war stories, guards shove him from the gate, and old soldiers slip him coin without meeting his eye.
habits: He salutes passing riders with a mocking flourish, taps his crutch against the stones to count the hours, and drinks whatever coin he gets before dusk.
secrets: He lost the leg while running away, not while charging.
He still keeps his old sword wrapped in oilcloth under the bridge.
He has a grown daughter in town who pretends not to know him.
lines: Spare a coin for a man who bled for the realm? Or at least for his ale?
Begging is a trade too. Stand still, look pitiful, remember the generous faces.
I marched for a lord once. He got a song. I got this stump. Fair trade, eh?
Laugh, go on. You will limp too one day, if you live long enough.
Brave, you say? Brave men are dead. I am just slow to die.
Left foot itches again. A foot I have not had for twelve winters. Bastard thing.

name: The Doom Preacher
description: Shouts prophecies of fire and judgment in the market square every day, terrified that if he ever falls silent he will have to face his own quiet doubts.
hook: Shouts prophecies of fire and judgment in the market square every day, terrified that if he ever falls silent he will have to face his own quiet doubts.
seen_by_others: Merchants call him a nuisance, old women bring him bread, and children mock his wild beard until he roars back at them.
habits: He climbs onto barrels to preach, points at random passers-by as examples of sin, and sleeps in temple porches wrapped in sackcloth.
secrets: He was a prosperous merchant once and lost everything at dice.
He has never once had the visions he describes so vividly.
He prays every night to be proven wrong about the end.
lines: You! Stranger! The road you walk ends at the same pit as all the others. Repent!
I preach because the heavens weep and nobody else will listen. Come closer.
Lords build towers and the heavens laugh. Every banner falls to dust.
Mock me, mock me. I have heard worse from my own conscience.
Do not praise me. Praise is the first seed of pride, and pride burns.
Tomorrow, maybe tomorrow the signs come. Or the day after. They must come.

name: The Guild Warden
description: Enforces every ancient guild rule with fanatical exactness, crushing outsiders and upstarts alike, because he believes rules are all that stand between his trade and ruin.
hook: Enforces every ancient guild rule with fanatical exactness, crushing outsiders and upstarts alike, because he believes rules are all that stand between his trade and ruin.
seen_by_others: Guild members respect and resent him; outsiders call him a locked gate who never takes a bribe and never lets anyone in.
habits: He quotes charters from memory, measures every apprentice's work with a brass rule, and inspects rival stalls on market days without asking leave.
secrets: He forged his own master's mark to earn his first guild seal.
His son wants to leave the trade and he cannot bear to hear it.
He secretly admires the outsider craftsmen he drives out of town.
lines: You are not from here. Then you will not sell here without the guild's leave.
Seven years apprentice, three journeyman, and then you may call yourself a master.
Lords tax us, wars starve us, but the guild endures. It always has.
Petty, am I? Then the charter is petty too. It has kept this town fed for generations.
You flatter well. Flattery does not count as a qualification.
Bent nails at the cooper's stall again. Fined, fined. Tomorrow.

name: The Caravan Broker
description: Brokers camel caravans across the desert, swearing oaths on his ancestors with every contract, and believes any deal that does not cheat someone slightly was badly negotiated.
hook: Brokers camel caravans across the desert, swearing oaths on his ancestors with every contract, and believes any deal that does not cheat someone slightly was badly negotiated.
seen_by_others: Merchants call him the honest liar, because his word always holds, but every one of his prices hides a story.
habits: He offers dates and water before any negotiation, never names the first price, and touches his heart and forehead whenever he swears by his grandfathers.
secrets: He has never personally crossed the deep desert he sells passage through.
He owes a fortune to a rival family he publicly despises.
The grandfathers he swears by were camel thieves, and he knows it.
lines: Peace upon you, guest. Sit in the shade, drink, and tell me what you seek.
Thirty camels, forty days, a guide who knows the wells. That is no small price, friend.
Emirs and kings change, but sand and thirst remain. My caravans outlive them all.
You insult me, you insult my grandfathers. They would have charged you double.
Such sweet words! Now I must give you a better price, and my children will starve.
Salt up, dates down, the southern road closed again... bad year, good profit.

name: The Proud Tanner
description: Works the stinking vats at the edge of town, shunned by every decent household, and has turned that exile into a fierce pride bordering on contempt for perfumed people.
hook: Works the stinking vats at the edge of town, shunned by every decent household, and has turned that exile into a fierce pride bordering on contempt for perfumed people.
seen_by_others: People hold their noses when he passes and buy his leather anyway; behind his back they call him the stink of the river.
habits: He deliberately shakes hands with those who flinch, discusses hides in vivid detail at meals, and never washes before visiting richer quarters.
secrets: He bathes in rosewater every feast day where nobody can see him.
He wanted to be a scribe but his father burned his only book.
He gives free boots to the town beggars every winter.
lines: Smell that? That is honest work. You will get used to it, or you will not.
Hides soak in dung and bark for months. Patience, stink, and then the finest leather.
Every lord rides on my saddles and sneers at my street. Funny, that.
Stinking? Aye. And richer than you, by the look of those boots.
Ha! Nobody praises a tanner. Are you sick, or do you want something?
Another batch spoiled by the rain. Curse the sky and its wet arse.

name: The Widow With the Ledger
description: Took over her late husband's trading house against every relative's wishes and runs it far better than he did, while pretending he left her precise instructions.
hook: Took over her late husband's trading house against every relative's wishes and runs it far better than he did, while pretending he left her precise instructions.
seen_by_others: Rivals underestimate her until the contracts close; her in-laws call her the usurper; her clerks would walk into fire for her.
habits: She wears mourning black years after the funeral, quotes her dead husband whenever she makes an unpopular decision, and reviews the accounts by candlelight every night.
secrets: Her husband left no instructions at all; she invents every single one.
She felt relief, not grief, on the morning he died.
She has refused two suitors to keep control of the house.
lines: Good day. My husband would have welcomed you, and so shall I. Briefly.
Wool at twelve, wine at nine, and no credit for anyone who owed my husband.
Wars raise the price of everything except mercy. We trade accordingly.
A woman cannot run this house? Odd, since I have run it for six years.
Kind. My husband always said flattery comes before a request. What is yours?
He would have sold. I will hold. He was usually wrong about wool.

name: The Horse Coper
description: Sells steppe horses to settled folk with dazzling patter, cheats townsmen without a flicker of shame, but would cut off his own hand before cheating a fellow rider.
hook: Sells steppe horses to settled folk with dazzling patter, cheats townsmen without a flicker of shame, but would cut off his own hand before cheating a fellow rider.
seen_by_others: City buyers swear his horses go lame the day after the sale, yet they keep coming back because nobody else has such mounts.
habits: He opens every horse's mouth while chatting, sleeps beside his herd rather than under a roof, and spits whenever someone praises town walls.
secrets: He dyes grey hairs on old mares to sell them as young ones.
He cannot sleep inside stone buildings without shaking.
He was driven from his clan for a killing he did not commit.
lines: You walk on your own feet? Shameful. Come, let me fix that for you.
This one runs all day and eats grass. Townsmen's horses eat silver and stumble.
Khans ride, emperors sit. That is why the steppe always wins in the end.
Cheat? I sold you a horse, friend. You bought it blind. That is your problem.
You have a good eye! Too bad you have a thin purse. Let us discuss.
Too many walls here. The air tastes of smoke and pigs. Three more days.

name: The Alewife
description: Brews the strongest ale in the quarter and rules her kitchen tavern like a queen, deciding by mood alone who drinks, who is thrown out, and who marries whom.
hook: Brews the strongest ale in the quarter and rules her kitchen tavern like a queen, deciding by mood alone who drinks, who is thrown out, and who marries whom.
seen_by_others: Men fear her ladle, women seek her advice, and nobody in the quarter dares start a fight under her roof.
habits: She tastes every batch with a wooden spoon she calls her judge, slaps drunks with a wet rag, and remembers every grudge from twenty years back.
secrets: She adds a bitter root to her ale to keep the regulars thirsty.
She once soured a cruel husband's cups for a year until he died.
She still loves the soldier who left her with child decades ago.
lines: Sit down, wipe your nose, and keep your hands off my daughters. Ale or broth?
Barley, water, time and a woman's patience. Men brew piss and call it ale.
Soldiers drink most and pay least. I keep a notched stick for each one.
Say that again and I will brew you into next week's batch.
Oh, get on with you. Flattery buys you nothing but a bigger cup. Fine.
Too sweet, that batch. Needs more bitterness. Like life.

name: The Battlefield Scavenger
description: Follows armies at a safe distance and strips the dead before the crows are finished, selling rings and boots with a cheerful shrug about how little corpses need them.
hook: Follows armies at a safe distance and strips the dead before the crows are finished, selling rings and boots with a cheerful shrug about how little corpses need them.
seen_by_others: Everyone buys from him and nobody admits it; soldiers spit when they see his cart, then haggle over the boots.
habits: He wears mismatched boots from many dead men, keeps teeth in a jar for the tooth-pullers, and hums funeral hymns while sorting his loot.
secrets: He once found his own brother among the dead and stripped him anyway.
He keeps one ring from every battle and cannot explain why.
He cannot sleep unless a lamp is burning beside him.
lines: Fine boots, stranger. Barely worn. The last owner will not mind, believe me.
After the battle, before the crows. That is when the honest trade happens.
Lords make the corpses, I just tidy up. So who is the vulture here?
Grave robber? I never dig. They lie right on top for me.
Kind words for a scavenger? You must want something cheap.
Rings, two. Buckles, six. One gold tooth. A decent little war, this one.

name: The Blue-Handed Dyer
description: Chases a perfect shade of blue he glimpsed once on a nobleman's cloak as a boy, ruining batches and fortunes and calling every failure a lesson.
hook: Chases a perfect shade of blue he glimpsed once on a nobleman's cloak as a boy, ruining batches and fortunes and calling every failure a lesson.
seen_by_others: Neighbors call him the mad dyer; clothiers admit his colors are unmatched, whenever he is willing to sell them.
habits: He holds fabric up to the sky at every hour of the day, stains everything he touches blue, and refuses to sell cloth he considers unfinished.
secrets: He stole his best recipe from his drowned master's notes.
He is slowly losing his sense of color and tells no one.
He owes money to half the dye merchants on the coast.
lines: Ah, a visitor. Do you see that? No, not the wall. The color. Look.
Woad, alum, piss and patience. Three months for one bolt worth showing.
Lords wear my blues to war and bleed on them. A waste of a good shade.
My hands are blue because they work. Yours are pale because they do not.
You like it? It is wrong. Too green. But thank you, I suppose.
Deeper. Deeper. Like the sea at dusk. Not this muddy rubbish.

name: The Generous Baker
description: Gives bread on credit to every hungry face in the quarter and is quietly drowning in debt, unable to stop because refusing someone feels worse than ruin.
hook: Gives bread on credit to every hungry face in the quarter and is quietly drowning in debt, unable to stop because refusing someone feels worse than ruin.
seen_by_others: The poor bless his name, other bakers despise him for spoiling prices, and his creditors are fast losing patience.
habits: He sneaks extra rolls into children's baskets, keeps a tally stick of debts he never collects, and rises long before dawn humming hymns.
secrets: He borrowed from the moneylender to keep the ovens burning.
His wife is quietly planning to leave him over the debts.
He once ruined a rival's oven out of envy and nobody ever knew.
lines: Fresh loaves, still warm! You look hungry. Take one, pay later, or never.
Flour, salt, fire, and getting up while the world is asleep. That is baking.
When armies come, bread doubles in price. I keep mine the same. Foolish, I know.
Cheat? Me? I give away half my bread. Ask anyone on this street.
Oh, stop, you will make me blush, and then the loaves burn.
Tally stick nearly full again. Need another stick. Need another miracle.

name: The Headman Who Bends
description: Has kept his village alive through three changes of lord by bowing lower than anyone, and believes pride is a luxury only the dead can afford.
hook: Has kept his village alive through three changes of lord by bowing lower than anyone, and believes pride is a luxury only the dead can afford.
seen_by_others: Lords think him servile, young men call him a coward, and the old women know he saved their children.
habits: He bows before speaking, offers bread and salt to every armed visitor, and keeps different banners hidden in his storehouse for each possible master.
secrets: He betrayed a rebellious neighbor to save the rest of the village.
He spits into the lord's tribute grain before sending it off.
He was brave once, and remembers exactly how that ended.
lines: Welcome, welcome, honored guest. The village is yours. Please, spare the barns.
Taxes gathered, roads cleared, wells clean. Whose taxes, this year? Ah. Yours.
Lords are like weather. You do not argue with rain, you thatch the roof.
Coward? Yes. And every child in this village lived through the last war.
Too kind, too kind. Now, how many sheep do your men need?
Which banner this spring... the blue, perhaps. Better dig out the blue.

name: The Petty Tyrant
description: Rules his village like a miniature kingdom, squeezing neighbors and dealing out favors, while groveling shamelessly before any real lord who rides through.
hook: Rules his village like a miniature kingdom, squeezing neighbors and dealing out favors, while groveling shamelessly before any real lord who rides through.
seen_by_others: Villagers obey him out of fear and owe him out of necessity; outsiders find him charming and slippery as an eel.
habits: He sits in the only chair in the village hall, makes petitioners wait on purpose, and keeps a list of who greeted him improperly.
secrets: He bought his position with a bribe to the lord's steward.
He is truly afraid of his own wife and her brothers.
He beats his dogs every time a lord humiliates him.
lines: Who sent you? Nobody speaks to anyone here without speaking to me first.
The well is mine, the mill is mine, the lord's favor is mine. Understand?
My lord, an honor, an honor. Anything you need, the village provides.
You dare? I could have you whipped before supper. Remember where you stand.
Yes, yes, a fine village, well run. I do my best, it is a burden.
The widow at the well did not bow today. Note it. Note it all.

name: The Grasping Freeholder
description: Buys his starving neighbors' fields after every bad harvest at a fraction of their worth, genuinely believing he is rescuing them from worse buyers.
hook: Buys his starving neighbors' fields after every bad harvest at a fraction of their worth, genuinely believing he is rescuing them from worse buyers.
seen_by_others: Neighbors call him a vulture, priests call him prudent, and his own sons call him stingy with their inheritance.
habits: He walks his field boundaries every morning, pays in grain rather than coin, and reminds everyone of the hungry year he helped them.
secrets: He moved two boundary stones during the last spring flood.
He dreams of marrying his daughter into a noble house.
He cannot read a single one of the deeds he collects.
lines: Good land around here, if you know how to keep it. Few do.
Bad harvest again on the south fields. I will offer a fair price. Fair for now.
Soldiers trample crops, lords tax harvests. Land survives both. Buy land.
Vulture? I paid him in grain when nobody else paid at all.
Wise, you say? Just patient. Patience owns half this valley.
Three more fields, and the meadow by the brook. Then the mill.

name: The Herb Seller
description: Sells remedies that are half genuine and half chalk and hope, and has convinced herself that belief heals as well as roots do, so her lies are merciful.
hook: Sells remedies that are half genuine and half chalk and hope, and has convinced herself that belief heals as well as roots do, so her lies are merciful.
seen_by_others: Some swear she saved their children, others that she sold them colored water; everyone visits her before any physician.
habits: She sniffs every customer's hands, mutters the names of remedies in an old tongue, and carries dried roots bundled into her hair.
secrets: She killed a patient with a wrong dose once and moved towns.
She tests every new mixture on herself first, sometimes badly.
She does not know the true names of half her herbs.
lines: You walk like a man with a sour belly. Come, I have just the thing.
Willow bark for pain, mint for wind, chalk for the hopeless. All help, in their way.
Soldiers bring me wounds, lords bring me gout. Swords and sweets, both kill.
Witch, is it? A witch would be richer and far less tired.
Oh, you are sweet. Sweet tongues need sage. Here, take some.
Too much nightshade, too little... no, no. Start again. Smaller dose.

name: The Cheerful Gravedigger
description: Digs the town's graves with unfailing good humor, treats death as an old friend who visits too often, and quietly measures every living person for their hole.
hook: Digs the town's graves with unfailing good humor, treats death as an old friend who visits too often, and quietly measures every living person for their hole.
seen_by_others: People cross the street to avoid his jokes, yet at funerals they find his calm strangely comforting.
habits: He whistles old drinking songs while digging, guesses people's heights aloud as they pass, and leaves wildflowers on the graves that nobody visits anymore.
secrets: He keeps a scratched list of who he expects to bury next.
He sold a pauper's corpse to a physician once for study.
He dug his own grave years ago and sits beside it on quiet evenings.
lines: Welcome to town! Tall fellow, aren't you? Six feet and a bit, I would say.
Deep enough for the dogs, shallow enough for my back. That is the art.
War is good for my trade and bad for my soul. Mostly good for trade.
Laugh at me, friend. I will be the last one laughing, eventually.
Kind words! I will remember them when I lay you down. Gently.
Another one this week. Busy, busy. Should raise my prices.

name: The Tavern Champion
description: An aging wrestler who hustles drunk strangers into bouts and wagers, still the strongest man in the alehouse but terrified of the day someone finally beats him.
hook: An aging wrestler who hustles drunk strangers into bouts and wagers, still the strongest man in the alehouse but terrified of the day someone finally beats him.
seen_by_others: Regulars cheer him like a lord, newcomers quickly learn to dodge his challenges, and the innkeeper takes a quiet share.
habits: He cracks his knuckles at every new face, arm-wrestles for drinks, and rubs his aching shoulder whenever he thinks nobody is watching.
secrets: He paid a younger man to lose to him last spring.
His back is failing and he hides the pain from everyone.
He cannot count and trusts the innkeeper's tally of his winnings blindly.
lines: New face! Strong arms? Let us see. One bout, one silver, winner drinks.
Grip the belt, plant the feet, and never let them see you are tired.
Lords hire champions with fancy swords. Give me the same ring and watch.
Say that outside. No, wait, say it in here. More witnesses.
Ha! Strongest man in town, they say. They say right. Buy me a cup.
Shoulder again. Damn shoulder. Two more winters. Just two more.

name: The Tavern Bard
